Chapter 12 — Clustering

Chapters 4 to 11 had the same ingredients: examples xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​ with labels yiy_iyi​, a loss that measures the disagreement between a prediction and a label, and a model class searched for a small loss. This chapter takes the labels away. With only the examples x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​, the question becomes whether they fall into groups, and what a good partition can mean when no label can say. The answer of clustering has a familiar form: choose the partition and the cluster centers that minimize the within-cluster sum of squares. For a fixed partition the best center of a cluster is, once more, its mean (Proposition 11.1 for the leaf of a tree is the same statement). We derive kkk-means and its guarantees, the criteria for choosing the number of clusters when there is no validation error to look at, the use of kkk-means as a compression method (vector quantization), Gaussian mixtures and hierarchical clustering as the first ways out of the spherical assumption, and spectral clustering, which replaces distances by a graph and eigenvectors by centers. The last section places clustering between supervised and unsupervised learning, with a handful of labels and many unlabeled examples.

12.1 Learning objectives¶

Part II of the book was about prediction. Part III is about structure: what can be learned from x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​ alone. The first difficulty is that there is no longer a loss that says what a correct answer is, and the chapter keeps coming back to it: every clustering algorithm is the minimization of some criterion, and the criterion carries the assumptions.

After working through the chapter you will be able to:

  1. formulate clustering as a combinatorial optimization problem over partitions, count the partitions (Stirling numbers), and prove that the pairwise-distance form of the within-cluster scatter equals the sum of squared distances to the cluster means, and that the total scatter splits into within and between parts;

  2. derive Lloyd’s algorithm for kkk-means from the two optimality conditions (nearest center, mean), prove that it decreases the objective and stops after finitely many steps at a point that is only a local minimum, and implement it from scratch;

  3. explain why the result depends on the initialization, prove the key lemma behind kkk-means++, and measure the spread of the local minima on real data;

  4. evaluate a clustering with an internal criterion (the silhouette) and with an external one (the adjusted Rand index, whose expected value under random labels is zero), and know what each can and cannot say;

  5. choose the number of clusters by the elbow, the silhouette, the gap statistic and the stability of the partition under resampling, and see on real data that these criteria disagree;

  6. read kkk-means as a vector quantizer, measure its rate–distortion curve on a photograph and on Digits, and relate the slope to an effective dimension;

  7. derive the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixtures, prove that it never decreases the likelihood, show that kkk-means is its limit when the variance goes to zero, and choose the covariance structure and the number of components with the BIC;

  8. derive agglomerative clustering, show that Ward’s criterion is the increase of the kkk-means objective at each merge, and explain the chaining of single linkage;

  9. define the graph Laplacian, prove that the multiplicity of the eigenvalue zero is the number of connected components, derive spectral clustering as the relaxation of the normalized cut, and run it on the nonconvex clusters where kkk-means fails and on Digits;

  10. compare supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised use of the same data: label propagation as the harmonic function of the graph, clusters as features, and the cases where unlabeled data help and where they do not.

We use four real data sets: Iris (150 flowers, 4 features, 3 species), Wine (178 wines, 13 chemical measurements, 3 cultivars; standardized), Breast Cancer (569 tumors, 30 features; standardized) and Digits (1797 images of 8×88\times88×8 pixels, 10 digits; pixels divided by 16). Two rules govern the whole chapter. First, the labels are never given to a clustering algorithm and never used to choose a hyperparameter; they are used afterwards, to score a partition, in the sections that say so (the species and the digits are what we hope the clusters recover, not what the algorithm was told). Second, clustering has no test set in the sense of the previous chapters: the whole data set is the training set, and we standardize it as a whole. In Section 12.9, where new points must be classified, we go back to the training/test split of Chapters 6 to 11 (1347/4501347/4501347/450 for Digits) and fit everything on the training part.

12.2 Clustering as a combinatorial problem¶

12.2.1 What is asked, and why it is not well defined¶

In a supervised problem the target yyy defines what a good answer is: it is the number the model will be scored against. In clustering the data are x1,…,xn∈Rp\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n\in\mathbb{R}^px1​,…,xn​∈Rp only, and the goal is a division into groups (“clusters”) such that the examples of a group are similar to one another and different from those of the other groups. Two things are missing from this sentence: the meaning of “similar”, and the number of groups. The Iris data show that both matter. The 150 flowers belong to three species, but only one species (setosa) is clearly separated from the other two in the four measurements, so that a partition into 2 groups is at least as natural as one into 3; and a partition into 3 groups that is natural for the measurements need not coincide with the species. A theorem of Kleinberg (2002) makes the difficulty precise: no clustering method can have at the same time three properties that look innocuous (invariance to the scale of the distances, the ability to produce any partition for a suitable choice of distances, and consistency, meaning that shrinking the distances inside the clusters and stretching those between them does not change the result). Every method is therefore a choice of what to give up, and the chapter is organized as a list of such choices.

12.2.2 Partitions and how many there are¶

Definition 12.1 (clustering)

A clustering of {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}{1,…,n} into kkk groups is a partition C={C1,…,Ck}\mathcal{C}=\{C_1,\dots,C_k\}C={C1​,…,Ck​} of the indices into kkk non-empty disjoint sets with union {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}{1,…,n}; equivalently, a map c:{1,…,n}→{1,…,k}c:\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,k\}c:{1,…,n}→{1,…,k} onto, with Cj={i:c(i)=j}C_j=\{i:c(i)=j\}Cj​={i:c(i)=j}. We write nj=∣Cj∣n_j=\lvert C_j\rvertnj​=∣Cj​∣ and μj=1nj∑i∈Cjxi\boldsymbol\mu_j=\frac1{n_j}\sum_{i\in C_j}\mathbf{x}_iμj​=nj​1​∑i∈Cj​​xi​ for the mean (the centroid) of the cluster jjj. The labels 1,…,k1,\dots,k1,…,k carry no meaning: two maps that differ by a permutation of the labels are the same clustering.

The number of such partitions is the Stirling number of the second kind S(n,k)S(n,k)S(n,k), which satisfies S(n,k)=k S(n−1,k)+S(n−1,k−1)S(n,k)=k\,S(n-1,k)+S(n-1,k-1)S(n,k)=kS(n−1,k)+S(n−1,k−1) (the point nnn either joins one of the kkk groups of a partition of the other n−1n-1n−1 points, or forms a group by itself) and grows like kn/k!k^n/k!kn/k!. Searching all partitions for the best one is out of the question, as the following code shows.

rows = []
for n, k in [(10, 3), (25, 3), (50, 3), (150, 3), (150, 5), (1797, 10)]:

    rows.append({"n": n, "k": k, "partitions S(n, k)": f"{float(s):.3e}" if len(str(s)) < 300 else f"10^{len(str(s)) - 1}",
                 "decimal digits": len(str(s))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
s150 = float(stirling2(150, 3, exact=True))
print(f"\nIris, k = 3: at 10^9 partitions per second, listing them takes {s150 / 1e9 / 3.156e7:.1e} years; "

12.2.3 A criterion: the within-cluster scatter¶

A criterion is needed to rank the partitions. The simplest asks that the squared Euclidean distance between two examples of the same cluster be small, summed over all the pairs of a cluster and over the clusters. To make clusters of different sizes comparable we divide by the size.

Definition 12.2 (scatter)

For a clustering C\mathcal{C}C of x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​, with xˉ\bar{\mathbf{x}}xˉ the mean of all the examples, define

SSW(C)=∑j=1k12nj∑i,i′∈Cj∥xi−xi′∥2,SSB(C)=∑j=1knj∥μj−xˉ∥2,SST=∑i=1n∥xi−xˉ∥2,\mathrm{SS}_W(\mathcal{C})=\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{2n_j}\sum_{i,i'\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_{i'}\rVert^2,\qquad \mathrm{SS}_B(\mathcal{C})=\sum_{j=1}^kn_j\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2,\qquad \mathrm{SS}_T=\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2,SSW​(C)=j=1∑k​2nj​1​i,i′∈Cj​∑​∥xi​−xi′​∥2,SSB​(C)=j=1∑k​nj​∥μj​−xˉ∥2,SST​=i=1∑n​∥xi​−xˉ∥2,
(1)

the within-cluster, between-cluster and total scatter (sums of squares). The total scatter does not depend on the clustering.

The first definition looks at pairs of examples, as the criteria of the combinatorial literature do; the next result turns it into a sum of squared distances to centers, which is the form we can optimize.

Proposition 12.1 (pairwise form and centroid form)

For every cluster CjC_jCj​ of a clustering,

12nj∑i,i′∈Cj∥xi−xi′∥2=∑i∈Cj∥xi−μj∥2,henceSSW(C)=∑j=1k∑i∈Cj∥xi−μj∥2.(12.1)\frac1{2n_j}\sum_{i,i'\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_{i'}\rVert^2=\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad \mathrm{SS}_W(\mathcal{C})=\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2.\tag{12.1}2nj​1​i,i′∈Cj​∑​∥xi​−xi′​∥2=i∈Cj​∑​∥xi​−μj​∥2,henceSSW​(C)=j=1∑k​i∈Cj​∑​∥xi​−μj​∥2.(12.1)
(2)

Proof. Write xi−xi′=(xi−μj)−(xi′−μj)\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_{i'}=(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j)-(\mathbf{x}_{i'}-\boldsymbol\mu_j)xi​−xi′​=(xi​−μj​)−(xi′​−μj​) and expand the square: ∑i,i′∥xi−xi′∥2=2nj∑i∥xi−μj∥2−2⟨∑i(xi−μj),∑i′(xi′−μj)⟩\sum_{i,i'}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_{i'}\rVert^2=2n_j\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2-2\big\langle\sum_i(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j),\sum_{i'}(\mathbf{x}_{i'}-\boldsymbol\mu_j)\big\rangle∑i,i′​∥xi​−xi′​∥2=2nj​∑i​∥xi​−μj​∥2−2⟨∑i​(xi​−μj​),∑i′​(xi′​−μj​)⟩, and the last term vanishes because the deviations from the mean sum to zero. ■\blacksquare■

The within-cluster scatter is therefore the sum of the squared distances of the examples to the mean of their cluster. The next result shows that it cannot be made smaller by a partition that ignores the position of the means, and that minimizing it is the same as maximizing the separation of the cluster means.

Proposition 12.2 (decomposition of the scatter; merging two clusters)

(a) For every clustering, SST=SSW(C)+SSB(C)\mathrm{SS}_T=\mathrm{SS}_W(\mathcal{C})+\mathrm{SS}_B(\mathcal{C})SST​=SSW​(C)+SSB​(C); since SST\mathrm{SS}_TSST​ is fixed, minimizing the within-cluster scatter is the same as maximizing the between-cluster scatter.

(b) If AAA and BBB are disjoint sets of examples with sizes nA,nBn_A,n_BnA​,nB​ and means μA,μB\boldsymbol\mu_A,\boldsymbol\mu_BμA​,μB​, then the scatter of A∪BA\cup BA∪B around its own mean exceeds the sum of the scatters of AAA and BBB around theirs by

SS(A∪B)−SS(A)−SS(B)=nAnBnA+nB ∥μA−μB∥2  ≥  0.(12.2)\mathrm{SS}(A\cup B)-\mathrm{SS}(A)-\mathrm{SS}(B)=\frac{n_An_B}{n_A+n_B}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2\;\ge\;0.\tag{12.2}SS(A∪B)−SS(A)−SS(B)=nA​+nB​nA​nB​​∥μA​−μB​∥2≥0.(12.2)
(3)

Merging two clusters never decreases the within-cluster scatter, and splitting one never increases it.

Proof. (a) For each cluster, ∑i∈Cj∥xi−xˉ∥2=∑i∈Cj∥xi−μj∥2+nj∥μj−xˉ∥2\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2=\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2+n_j\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2∑i∈Cj​​∥xi​−xˉ∥2=∑i∈Cj​​∥xi​−μj​∥2+nj​∥μj​−xˉ∥2 (add and subtract μj\boldsymbol\mu_jμj​; the cross term has zero sum). Sum over jjj. (b) Apply (a) to the data set A∪BA\cup BA∪B with the two clusters AAA and BBB: the difference in (12.2) is the between-cluster scatter nA∥μA−μ∥2+nB∥μB−μ∥2n_A\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert^2+n_B\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_B-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert^2nA​∥μA​−μ∥2+nB​∥μB​−μ∥2, with μ=(nAμA+nBμB)/(nA+nB)\boldsymbol\mu=(n_A\boldsymbol\mu_A+n_B\boldsymbol\mu_B)/(n_A+n_B)μ=(nA​μA​+nB​μB​)/(nA​+nB​). Since μA−μ=nBnA+nB(μA−μB)\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu=\frac{n_B}{n_A+n_B}(\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B)μA​−μ=nA​+nB​nB​​(μA​−μB​) and μB−μ=−nAnA+nB(μA−μB)\boldsymbol\mu_B-\boldsymbol\mu=-\frac{n_A}{n_A+n_B}(\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B)μB​−μ=−nA​+nB​nA​​(μA​−μB​), the sum is nAnB2+nBnA2(nA+nB)2∥μA−μB∥2=nAnBnA+nB∥μA−μB∥2\frac{n_An_B^2+n_Bn_A^2}{(n_A+n_B)^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2=\frac{n_An_B}{n_A+n_B}\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2(nA​+nB​)2nA​nB2​+nB​nA2​​∥μA​−μB​∥2=nA​+nB​nA​nB​​∥μA​−μB​∥2. ■\blacksquare■

Equation (12.2) is exactly Proposition 11.2, the gain of a split in a regression tree, with the targets replaced by vectors: a tree that splits a node and a clustering algorithm that splits or merges a cluster are measuring the same quantity, the squared distance between the two means weighted by nAnB/(nA+nB)n_An_B/(n_A+n_B)nA​nB​/(nA​+nB​). The two problems differ in what they are allowed to do: the tree chooses the two groups with a threshold on one feature, because the targets have to be predicted from the features, whereas a clustering may put any examples together.

The following code checks Proposition 12.1 and Proposition 12.2 on Iris with a random partition into three groups, and with the partition given by the species, which we use here only to see how much of the scatter it explains.

def ss_within(X, labels):
    """Within-cluster scatter in the centroid form (12.1)."""
    return float(sum(((X[labels == j] - X[labels == j].mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum() for j in np.unique(labels)))


def ss_within_pairs(X, labels):
    """The same quantity in the pairwise form of Definition 12.2."""
    total = 0.0
    for j in np.unique(labels):
        Z = X[labels == j]
        total += ((Z[:, None, :] - Z[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum() / (2 * len(Z))
    return float(total)


def ss_between(X, labels):
    xbar = X.mean(axis=0)
    return float(sum((labels == j).sum() * ((X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) - xbar) ** 2).sum() for j in np.unique(labels)))


ss_total = float(((X_iris - X_iris.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum())
rand_labels = np.random.default_rng(SEED).integers(0, 3, len(X_iris))
for name, lab in [("random partition", rand_labels), ("species", y_iris)]:
    w_c, w_p, b = ss_within(X_iris, lab), ss_within_pairs(X_iris, lab), ss_between(X_iris, lab)
    print(f"{name:17s} SS_W centroid form {w_c:9.4f}   pairwise form {w_p:9.4f}   |difference| {abs(w_c - w_p):.1e}"
          f"   SS_W + SS_B - SS_T = {w_c + b - ss_total:+.1e}")
print(f"SS_T = {ss_total:.2f};  species: SS_W / SS_T = {ss_within(X_iris, y_iris) / ss_total:.3f},"
      f"  random: {ss_within(X_iris, rand_labels) / ss_total:.3f}")

# Proposition 12.2(b): merging setosa (class 0) and versicolor (class 1)
A, B = X_iris[y_iris == 0], X_iris[y_iris == 1]
lhs = ss_within(np.vstack([A, B]), np.zeros(100, int)) - ss_within(A, np.zeros(50, int)) - ss_within(B, np.zeros(50, int))
rhs = len(A) * len(B) / (len(A) + len(B)) * ((A.mean(axis=0) - B.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum()
print(f"\nmerging setosa and versicolor: increase of the scatter {lhs:.4f}, formula (12.2) {rhs:.4f}")
random partition  SS_W centroid form  675.0583   pairwise form  675.0583   |difference| 0.0e+00   SS_W + SS_B - SS_T = +0.0e+00
species           SS_W centroid form   89.2974   pairwise form   89.2974   |difference| 1.4e-14   SS_W + SS_B - SS_T = -1.1e-13
SS_T = 681.37;  species: SS_W / SS_T = 0.131,  random: 0.991

The two forms of the within-cluster scatter agree to rounding error (1.4×10−141.4\times10^{-14}1.4×10−14 at most), and the decomposition of Proposition 12.2(a) holds to the same precision. The two partitions could hardly differ more. A random partition into three groups has SSW/SST=0.991\mathrm{SS}_W/\mathrm{SS}_T=0.991SSW​/SST​=0.991: it explains less than 1%1\%1% of the scatter, as it must, because each random group of about 50 flowers has almost the same mean as the whole sample. The species have SSW=89.30\mathrm{SS}_W=89.30SSW​=89.30, which is 13.1%13.1\%13.1% of SST=681.37\mathrm{SS}_T=681.37SST​=681.37, so the three species account for 86.9%86.9\%86.9% of the scatter of the four measurements. Merging setosa and versicolor raises the scatter by 257.33, the value that equation (12.2) predicts, to all the digits printed.

The species partition is not the partition that minimizes SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​: the best partition into three groups, found below, has SSW=78.85\mathrm{SS}_W=78.85SSW​=78.85, lower than the 89.30 of the species. A clustering algorithm optimizes a criterion, not the labels, and the two can disagree; we come back to this in Section 12.4.

12.2.4 A hard problem¶

Minimizing SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ over the partitions into kkk groups is the kkk-means problem. It is NP-hard when the dimension is not fixed, even for k=2k=2k=2 (Aloise, Deshpande, Hansen and Popat, 2009), and also in the plane when kkk is not fixed (Mahajan, Nimbhorkar and Varadarajan, 2012), the analogue for partitions of the NP-completeness of the optimal tree quoted in Section 11.2.2. No algorithm is known that finds the best partition in time polynomial in nnn, kkk and ppp for all data sets, and the practical algorithms of the chapter are therefore heuristics: local search methods that reach a partition that cannot be improved by simple moves, with no promise that it is the best one. The same situation was met in Chapter 7 (nonconvex objectives) and Chapter 11 (greedy trees), and the remedy will be the same: understand what the algorithm guarantees, run it from several starting points, and look at how much the answer depends on them.

12.3 kkk-means¶

12.3.1 Two optimality conditions¶

Because of Proposition 12.1 we can minimize over the centers as well as over the partition. For centers μ1,…,μk∈Rp\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k\in\mathbb{R}^pμ1​,…,μk​∈Rp and an assignment c(i)∈{1,…,k}c(i)\in\{1,\dots,k\}c(i)∈{1,…,k} define the kkk-means objective

J(c,μ1,…,μk)=∑i=1n∥xi−μc(i)∥2.(12.3)J(c,\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_{c(i)}\rVert^2.\tag{12.3}J(c,μ1​,…,μk​)=i=1∑n​∥xi​−μc(i)​∥2.(12.3)
(4)
Proposition 12.3 (the two optimality conditions)

(a) For fixed centers, JJJ is minimized over the assignments by sending each example to its nearest center, c(i)∈arg⁡min⁡j∥xi−μj∥c(i)\in\arg\min_j\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVertc(i)∈argminj​∥xi​−μj​∥. The set of points closer to μj\boldsymbol\mu_jμj​ than to every other center is a polyhedron (a Voronoi cell) bounded by hyperplanes that are the perpendicular bisectors of the segments between centers.

(b) For a fixed assignment, JJJ is minimized over the centers by the means of the clusters, μj=1nj∑i∈Cjxi\boldsymbol\mu_j=\frac1{n_j}\sum_{i\in C_j}\mathbf{x}_iμj​=nj​1​∑i∈Cj​​xi​ (any point for an empty cluster).

(c) Hence min⁡c,μJ=min⁡CSSW(C)\min_{c,\boldsymbol\mu}J=\min_{\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{SS}_W(\mathcal{C})minc,μ​J=minC​SSW​(C), the minimum over the partitions into at most kkk groups, and every global minimizer satisfies (a) and (b) at the same time.

Proof. (a) JJJ is a sum of nnn terms, the iii-th depending only on c(i)c(i)c(i), so each term is minimized separately. The cell of μj\boldsymbol\mu_jμj​ is defined by the inequalities ∥x−μj∥2≤∥x−μl∥2\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2\le\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_l\rVert^2∥x−μj​∥2≤∥x−μl​∥2, which are linear in x\mathbf{x}x: 2⟨x,μl−μj⟩≤∥μl∥2−∥μj∥22\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\mu_l-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rangle\le\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_l\rVert^2-\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^22⟨x,μl​−μj​⟩≤∥μl​∥2−∥μj​∥2. (b) JJJ splits into one sum per cluster, and in cluster jjj the function μ↦∑i∈Cj∥xi−μ∥2\boldsymbol\mu\mapsto\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert^2μ↦∑i∈Cj​​∥xi​−μ∥2 is a convex quadratic with gradient −2∑i∈Cj(xi−μ)-2\sum_{i\in C_j}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)−2∑i∈Cj​​(xi​−μ), which vanishes at the mean; this is the argument of Proposition 11.1. (c) By (b) and Proposition 12.1 the minimum over the centers of JJJ is SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​; a global minimizer of JJJ must be a minimizer in each of the two blocks of variables. ■\blacksquare■

Two remarks. The statement (b) is Proposition 11.1 again: the value in the box of a regression tree and the center of a cluster are both means, because both problems minimize a sum of squares. And (a) says that a kkk-means partition is a partition into convex regions whose boundaries are hyperplanes, exactly as a tree’s boxes are axis-aligned boxes: a tree is a partition chosen with the targets, in boxes, by greedy splitting; kkk-means is a partition chosen without targets, in Voronoi cells, by alternating the two conditions of the proposition. That alternation is the algorithm.

12.3.2 Lloyd’s algorithm¶

Lloyd’s algorithm (1957, published in 1982; also called the kkk-means algorithm) starts from kkk centers and repeats two steps until the assignment no longer changes:

  1. assignment step: send every example to its nearest center, keeping its current cluster unless another center is strictly nearer;

  2. update step: replace each center by the mean of its cluster (an empty cluster keeps its center).

The assignment step costs O(nkp)O(nkp)O(nkp) operations (the squared distances are ∥x∥2−2⟨x,μ⟩+∥μ∥2\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2-2\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\mu\rangle+\lVert\boldsymbol\mu\rVert^2∥x∥2−2⟨x,μ⟩+∥μ∥2, a matrix product), the update step O(np)O(np)O(np).

Theorem 12.4 (Lloyd’s algorithm)

Let JtJ_tJt​ be the value of (12.3) after the update step of iteration ttt. Then Jt+1≤JtJ_{t+1}\le J_tJt+1​≤Jt​, with strict inequality whenever the assignment changes, and the algorithm stops after a finite number of iterations at a pair (assignment, centers) that satisfies both conditions of Proposition 12.3. That pair is in general not a global minimizer of JJJ.

Proof. By Proposition 12.3(a) the assignment step does not increase JJJ, and it decreases it strictly if some example moves to a strictly nearer center; by 12.3(b) the update step does not increase JJJ. Hence JJJ never increases, and strictly decreases whenever the assignment changes. A partition cannot occur twice with a strict decrease in between, and there are finitely many partitions, so the assignment stops changing; at that moment the centers are the means of the clusters and every example is at least as near to its own center as to any other. That a fixed point need not be a global minimum is shown by examples as small as four points (Exercise 12.1), and by the experiments of the next subsection. ■\blacksquare■

The theorem is a statement about monotone decrease and termination; it says nothing about the quality of the point reached, and nothing about the number of iterations, which can be large in the worst case (superpolynomial examples exist) but is a few tens in practice. The following code implements the algorithm and compares it with scikit-learn started from the same three centers (three Iris flowers chosen at random).

def lloyd(X, centers, max_iter=300):
    """Lloyd's algorithm. Returns centers, labels, the history of J and the history of the centers."""
    C = np.array(centers, dtype=float)
    labels, J_hist, C_hist = None, [], [C.copy()]
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        D = (X ** 2).sum(1)[:, None] - 2 * X @ C.T + (C ** 2).sum(1)[None, :]       # squared distances, n x k
        new = D.argmin(axis=1)
        if labels is not None:                       # keep the current cluster unless another center is strictly nearer
            keep = D[np.arange(len(X)), labels] <= D[np.arange(len(X)), new] + 1e-12
            new = np.where(keep, labels, new)
        J_hist.append(float(((X - C[new]) ** 2).sum()))
        if labels is not None and (new == labels).all():
            break
        labels = new
        for j in range(len(C)):
            if (labels == j).any():
                C[j] = X[labels == j].mean(axis=0)
        C_hist.append(C.copy())
    return C, labels, J_hist, C_hist


init_idx = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(len(X_iris), 3, replace=False)
C0 = X_iris[init_idx]
C_fin, lab_fin, J_hist, _ = lloyd(X_iris, C0)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init=C0, n_init=1, algorithm="lloyd", tol=0, max_iter=300).fit(X_iris)
print("J after each assignment step:", " ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in J_hist))
print(f"monotone: {bool(np.all(np.diff(J_hist) <= 1e-9))};  assignment steps (the last one finds that nothing changes): ours {len(J_hist)}, scikit-learn {km.n_iter_}")
print(f"final J: ours {J_hist[-1]:.6f}, scikit-learn {km.inertia_:.6f};  largest difference of the centers "
      f"{np.abs(np.sort(C_fin, axis=0) - np.sort(km.cluster_centers_, axis=0)).max():.1e}")
J after each assignment step: 181.27 88.83 84.95 84.01 83.05 81.75 80.81 79.87 79.34 78.92 78.86
monotone: True;  assignment steps (the last one finds that nothing changes): ours 11, scikit-learn 11
final J: ours 78.855666, scikit-learn 78.855666;  largest difference of the centers 1.8e-15

The two implementations follow the same path. Started from the same three flowers they stop at J=78.855666J=78.855666J=78.855666 with centers that agree to 1.8×10−151.8\times10^{-15}1.8×10−15, after the same number of assignment steps (11, the last one being the step that finds that nothing changes). The objective decreases at every step, as Theorem 12.4 says: it is 181.27 after the first assignment, 88.83 after the second, and the nine remaining steps lower it by ten units more, in irregular steps, the last of which is 0.06. The value reached is not the lowest of the chapter: other starts reach 78.851 (Section 12.3.4), a different fixed point 0.005 lower. Theorem 12.4 guarantees a fixed point, not the best one.

Figure 12.1 shows the algorithm on two of the four features (the petal length and width, so that the picture is the whole problem), started from three flowers chosen at random. The color is the cluster, the marker shape is the species, which the algorithm never sees.

def figure_12_1():
    Xp = X_iris[:, 2:4]
    idx = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 3).choice(len(Xp), 3, replace=False)
    C, lab, J_h, C_h = lloyd(Xp, Xp[idx])
    steps = [0, 1, 2, len(C_h) - 1]
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0.6, 7.2, 300), np.linspace(-0.05, 2.75, 300))
    grid = np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()]
    markers = ["o", "s", "^"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, t in zip(axes, steps):
        Ct = C_h[t]
        cell = ((grid[:, None, :] - Ct[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1).reshape(gx.shape)
        ax.contourf(gx, gy, cell, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5], colors=CLUSTER_COLORS[:3], alpha=0.15)
        assign = ((Xp[:, None, :] - Ct[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)
        for s in range(3):
            m = y_iris == s
            ax.scatter(Xp[m, 0], Xp[m, 1], c=[CLUSTER_COLORS[a] for a in assign[m]], marker=markers[s], s=26, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
        ax.scatter(Ct[:, 0], Ct[:, 1], c="black", marker="X", s=110, edgecolor="white", zorder=5)
        j_t = float(((Xp - Ct[assign]) ** 2).sum())
        ax.set_title(("initial centers" if t == 0 else f"after update {t}" if t < len(C_h) - 1 else f"converged ({t} updates)") + f"\nJ = {j_t:.1f}")
        ax.set_xlabel("petal length (cm)")
        ax.grid(False)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("petal width (cm)")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_1()

The figure shows what the theorem does not say, namely how a bad start is repaired. The three initial centers are flowers of the two large species and none is near setosa, so in the first panel every setosa flower is assigned to the center in the middle of the picture, together with the small versicolor flowers. The update moves this center toward the mean of that mixed group, and then, one step after another, to the left, until it sits on setosa while the other two centers divide versicolor and virginica between them. The objective on the two features goes from 588.1 to 219.4, 95.8 and 31.4 at the end (9 updates). The squares and triangles of a different color from their neighbors, at the boundary between the two large species, are flowers that the partition places in the other cluster than their species; there is no line that separates the two species without errors in these two features.

12.3.3 A fixed point can still be improved¶

The conditions of Proposition 12.3 are conditions on two blocks of variables, and they are weaker than optimality with respect to every change of the partition. Moving one example x\mathbf{x}x from the cluster AAA (with nAn_AnA​ points and mean μA\boldsymbol\mu_AμA​) to the cluster BBB (with nBn_BnB​ points and mean μB\boldsymbol\mu_BμB​) and recomputing the two means changes the objective by

ΔJ=nBnB+1∥x−μB∥2−nAnA−1∥x−μA∥2,\Delta J=\frac{n_B}{n_B+1}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2-\frac{n_A}{n_A-1}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_A\rVert^2,ΔJ=nB​+1nB​​∥x−μB​∥2−nA​−1nA​​∥x−μA​∥2,
(5)

(the two terms are the increase of the scatter of BBB when it gains x\mathbf{x}x and the decrease of the scatter of AAA when it loses it; both are instances of equation (12.2) in which one of the two sets is the single point x\mathbf{x}x). Lloyd’s algorithm compares ∥x−μB∥2\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2∥x−μB​∥2 with ∥x−μA∥2\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_A\rVert^2∥x−μA​∥2 without the two factors, which are larger and smaller than 1 respectively, so it can stop at a partition in which a single move still decreases JJJ. The algorithm of Hartigan and Wong (1979), which tests ΔJ\Delta JΔJ, avoids this. How often does it happen? We run Lloyd’s algorithm (scikit-learn’s) on Digits with k=10k=10k=10 and test every example against every other cluster.

def best_single_moves(X, labels, centers):
    """For each example, the smallest change of J obtained by moving it to another cluster (negative = improvement)."""
    k = len(centers)
    n_j = np.bincount(labels, minlength=k).astype(float)
    D = ((X[:, None, :] - centers[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    own = D[np.arange(len(X)), labels]
    leave = n_j[labels] / np.maximum(n_j[labels] - 1, 1) * own            # decrease of J if x leaves its cluster
    join = n_j[None, :] / (n_j[None, :] + 1) * D                            # increase of J if x joins cluster j
    join[np.arange(len(X)), labels] = np.inf
    best = join.argmin(axis=1)
    return join[np.arange(len(X)), best] - leave, best


rows = []
for seed in range(3):
    km = KMeans(10, n_init=1, init="random", random_state=seed, tol=0).fit(X_dig)
    delta, target = best_single_moves(X_dig, km.labels_, km.cluster_centers_)
    i = int(delta.argmin())
    moved = km.labels_.copy(); moved[i] = target[i]
    J_before = ss_within(X_dig, km.labels_); J_after = ss_within(X_dig, moved)             # recomputed with the new means
    rows.append({"seed": seed, "J at the fixed point": J_before, "examples whose move helps": int((delta < -1e-9).sum()),
                 "best predicted change": delta[i], "change of J after the move": J_after - J_before})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
 seed  J at the fixed point  examples whose move helps  best predicted change  change of J after the move
    0             4592.4535                          6                -0.0454                     -0.0454
    1             4628.7339                          5                -0.0598                     -0.0598
    2             4824.6555                          4                -0.0585                     -0.0585

The single-move formula is exact: the change of JJJ predicted by ΔJ\Delta JΔJ and the change computed after moving the example and recomputing the two means are the same to four decimals (-0.0454, -0.0598, -0.0585). The three fixed points of Lloyd’s algorithm contain 6, 5 and 4 examples whose move lowers the objective, so the fixed points of Proposition 12.3 are not locally optimal for single moves. But the amount is small: the best single move improves JJJ by about 0.05 out of 4600, one part in 105. In practice the difference between Lloyd and Hartigan–Wong is negligible next to the difference between local minima: these three runs end at 4592.5, 4628.7 and 4824.7, that is 0.9%0.9\%0.9%, 1.7%1.7\%1.7% and 6.0%6.0\%6.0% above the best value found for Digits with k=10k=10k=10 (see the next table). What matters for the result is where the algorithm starts.

12.3.4 Local minima and the initialization¶

Lloyd’s algorithm is deterministic given the initial centers, so the quality of the result is decided by the initialization. The simplest choice, kkk examples chosen uniformly at random, can put two centers in the same natural group and leave another group without one, a situation from which the two steps cannot escape. kkk-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) spreads the initial centers by sampling:

  1. choose the first center uniformly among the examples;

  2. for each example let D(x)2D(\mathbf{x})^2D(x)2 be the squared distance to the nearest center chosen so far, and choose the next center among the examples with probability proportional to D(x)2D(\mathbf{x})^2D(x)2;

  3. repeat step 2 until kkk centers have been chosen, and then run Lloyd’s algorithm.

An example far from all the chosen centers has a large D2D^2D2 and is likely to be chosen, so the new centers tend to fall in groups that do not yet have one. The analysis rests on the following lemma, which says how good a single uniformly chosen center is for the cluster that contains it.

Lemma 12.5 (a random center costs twice the optimum)

Let AAA be a set of nAn_AnA​ points with mean μA\boldsymbol\mu_AμA​ and let c\mathbf{c}c be drawn uniformly from AAA. Then

E[∑x∈A∥x−c∥2]=2∑x∈A∥x−μA∥2.\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}\rVert^2\Big]=2\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_A\rVert^2 .E[x∈A∑​∥x−c∥2]=2x∈A∑​∥x−μA​∥2.
(6)

Proof. For every point c\mathbf{c}c, ∑x∈A∥x−c∥2=∑x∈A∥x−μA∥2+nA∥μA−c∥2\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}\rVert^2=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A}\lVert\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_A\rVert^2+n_A\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\mathbf{c}\rVert^2∑x∈A​∥x−c∥2=∑x∈A​∥x−μA​∥2+nA​∥μA​−c∥2 (add and subtract μA\boldsymbol\mu_AμA​). Average over c∈A\mathbf{c}\in Ac∈A: the second term becomes nA⋅1nA∑c∈A∥c−μA∥2n_A\cdot\frac1{n_A}\sum_{\mathbf{c}\in A}\lVert\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol\mu_A\rVert^2nA​⋅nA​1​∑c∈A​∥c−μA​∥2, equal to the optimal scatter again. ■\blacksquare■

Applied to every optimal cluster in turn, with the D2D^2D2 sampling making it likely that a new center falls in a cluster not yet covered, the lemma is the core of the main result.

Theorem 12.6 (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007; stated without proof)

The expected value of JJJ for the centers chosen by kkk-means++ (before any Lloyd iteration) is at most 8(ln⁡k+2)8(\ln k+2)8(lnk+2) times the optimal value of JJJ.

The guarantee is on the seeding alone, it grows only logarithmically with kkk, and Lloyd’s iterations can only improve it by Theorem 12.4. No guarantee of this kind exists for the uniform seeding (Exercise 12.1 is an example in which the ratio is unbounded). The next code checks the lemma on the 50 versicolor flowers (the average over all 50 possible choices of c\mathbf{c}c is exactly computable), implements kkk-means++ and measures how often the two seedings reach the best value found, on three data sets, in 200 runs of a single start each.

Z = X_iris[y_iris == 1]
opt_one = ((Z - Z.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum()
mean_cost = np.mean([((Z - c) ** 2).sum() for c in Z])             # exact average over the 50 possible centers
print(f"Lemma 12.5 on 50 versicolor flowers: average cost of a uniform center {mean_cost:.4f}, twice the optimum {2 * opt_one:.4f}")


def kmeans_pp_seeds(X, k, rng):
    """k-means++ seeding, as in the three steps above."""
    centers = [X[rng.integers(len(X))]]
    for _ in range(k - 1):
        d2 = ((X[:, None, :] - np.array(centers)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).min(axis=1)
        centers.append(X[rng.choice(len(X), p=d2 / d2.sum())])
    return np.array(centers)


# Our seeding followed by our Lloyd, 200 starts on Iris, against uniform seeding
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
J_pp = [lloyd(X_iris, kmeans_pp_seeds(X_iris, 3, rng))[2][-1] for _ in range(200)]
J_rand = [lloyd(X_iris, X_iris[rng.choice(len(X_iris), 3, replace=False)])[2][-1] for _ in range(200)]
print(f"Iris, k = 3, 200 starts of our code: k-means++ seeding gives J in [{min(J_pp):.2f}, {max(J_pp):.2f}] and ends in the bad local minimum (J > 100) in {sum(v > 100 for v in J_pp)} runs; "
      f"uniform seeding gives J in [{min(J_rand):.2f}, {max(J_rand):.2f}] and {sum(v > 100 for v in J_rand)} bad runs")

# The three data sets with scikit-learn's implementations: 200 runs with a single start each
init_study = {}
for name, k in [("Iris", 3), ("Wine", 3), ("Digits", 10)]:
    X = datasets[name][0]
    init_study[name] = {init: np.array([KMeans(k, init=init, n_init=1, random_state=s).fit(X).inertia_ for s in range(200)])
                        for init in ["random", "k-means++"]}
rows = []
for name, d in init_study.items():
    best = min(v.min() for v in d.values())
    for init, v in d.items():
        hit = float((v <= best * (1 + 1e-3)).mean())
        rows.append({"data": name, "seeding": init, "best J": v.min(), "median J": np.median(v), "worst J": v.max(),
                     "runs within 0.1% of the best": hit, "P(hit in 10 starts)": 1 - (1 - hit) ** 10})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}" if v < 100 else f"{v:.1f}"))
Lemma 12.5 on 50 versicolor flowers: average cost of a uniform center 61.2328, twice the optimum 61.2328
Iris, k = 3, 200 starts of our code: k-means++ seeding gives J in [78.85, 145.53] and ends in the bad local minimum (J > 100) in 19 runs; uniform seeding gives J in [78.85, 145.76] and 49 bad runs

  data   seeding  best J  median J  worst J  runs within 0.1% of the best  P(hit in 10 starts)
  Iris    random  78.851    78.856    145.8                         0.785                1.000
  Iris k-means++  78.851    78.856   78.856                         1.000                1.000
  Wine    random  1277.9    1278.8   1617.4                         0.575                1.000

The lemma holds exactly: the average cost of a uniform center on the 50 versicolor flowers is 61.2328, twice the optimal scatter of the group.

The results do not say that kkk-means++ is always better. On Iris, with our plain implementation of the three steps, 19 of the 200 runs end in one of the bad local minima (JJJ between 142.7 and 145.8, all of them with setosa split in two and versicolor and virginica merged) against 49 for uniform seeding, which is a reduction of more than half but not a cure. The implementation of scikit-learn uses a greedy variant, which draws several candidate centers at each step and keeps the one that lowers JJJ most; with it, all 200 runs reach the best value on Iris. On Wine the two seedings are indistinguishable (57.5%57.5\%57.5% and 52.0%52.0\%52.0% of the runs within 0.1%0.1\%0.1% of the best value, a difference of ten runs out of two hundred, about one standard error); a few runs of both end about 25%25\%25% above the best, with one cluster badly placed. On Digits, where the landscape has many local minima, kkk-means++ is clearly better: 37%37\%37% of the runs against 21%21\%21% reach the best value, the median is 0.4%0.4\%0.4% above the best against 0.6%0.6\%0.6%, and ten starts contain a run within 0.1%0.1\%0.1% of the best with probability 0.990 against 0.905 (computed from the table as 1−(1−p)101-(1-p)^{10}1−(1−p)10 under independence of starts).

Two practical rules follow. First, the number of starts matters as much as the seeding: a success probability of 0.2 per start becomes 0.9 with ten starts, which is why the algorithm is normally run several times and the partition with the smallest JJJ is kept (scikit-learn’s default, n_init='auto', runs 10 starts with uniform seeding and a single one with kkk-means++; the Digits rows show what that single start can miss). Second, the value “best JJJ found” is a proxy for the optimum: none of the 400 runs certifies that no better partition exists.

def figure_12_2():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
    for ax, (name, d) in zip(axes, init_study.items()):
        best = min(v.min() for v in d.values())
        for pos, (init, v) in enumerate(d.items()):
            jitter = np.random.default_rng(pos).uniform(-0.18, 0.18, len(v))
            ax.scatter(pos + jitter, v / best, s=14, alpha=0.55, color=[BLUE, ORANGE][pos], marker=["o", "s"][pos])
            ax.hlines(np.median(v) / best, pos - 0.3, pos + 0.3, color="black", linewidth=2)
        ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["uniform seeding", "k-means++"])
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 1.6)
        ax.set_title(f"{name}")
        ax.set_ylabel("J / best J found" if name == "Iris" else "")
    fig.suptitle("200 single starts: final objective relative to the best value found (black bar = median)", y=1.02)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_2()

Figure 12.2 shows the same 200 runs. On Iris the uniform seeding yields two groups of values, the best one and a group at 1.81 to 1.85 times the best (the partitions with setosa split in two), and nothing in between; the dispersion is a matter of which local minimum, not of how far from it. On Wine the bad starts are rare. On Digits there is no bad group but a continuum of local minima, up to 8%8\%8% above the best, and the two seedings differ in how the values are distributed, not in the range.

12.3.5 The scale of the features decides the clusters¶

kkk-means uses the Euclidean distance, so a feature with a large range dominates the distances, as in kkk-NN (Chapter 4) and in the SVM (Chapter 8). On Wine the effect is dramatic. The raw features have very different scales (the proline content is in the hundreds, the hue near 1), and the partition of the raw data is almost entirely a partition by proline. We score the partitions with the adjusted Rand index (ARI) of Section 12.4, which is 1 when the partition equals the cultivars and about 0 for a partition unrelated to them.

rows = []
for name, X in [("raw features", wine.data), ("standardized", X_wine), ("min-max scaled", (wine.data - wine.data.min(0)) / np.ptp(wine.data, axis=0))]:
    labs = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X)
    rows.append({"features": name, "ARI with the cultivars": adjusted_rand_score(y_wine, labs),
                 "share of the variance of the largest-scale feature": X.var(axis=0).max() / X.var(axis=0).sum()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
print("raw features with the largest standard deviation:", ", ".join(f"{wine.feature_names[j]} ({wine.data[:, j].std():.1f})" for j in np.argsort(-wine.data.std(axis=0))[:3]))
      features  ARI with the cultivars  share of the variance of the largest-scale feature
  raw features                   0.371                                               0.998
  standardized                   0.897                                               0.077
min-max scaled                   0.854                                               0.125
raw features with the largest standard deviation: proline (314.0), magnesium (14.2), alcalinity_of_ash (3.3)

The scale is decisive. With the raw measurements one feature, the proline, carries 99.8%99.8\%99.8% of the total variance, so the Euclidean distance between two wines is practically the difference between their proline values, and the partition is a partition of that one axis: ARI 0.371. Standardizing, which gives every feature the same variance (1/131/131/13 of the total, 7.7%7.7\%7.7%), raises the ARI to 0.897. Min-max scaling, which brings every feature to [0,1][0,1][0,1], is intermediate (0.854) because the range of a feature is set by its extreme values, and an outlier can make a feature count less than the others. There is no scale-free answer: the choice of scale states how much each feature matters, and standardization, which says that a standard deviation counts the same in every feature, is the default used in the rest of the chapter for Wine and Breast Cancer.

Beyond the scale, kkk-means makes three assumptions that follow from (12.3): the clusters are convex (Voronoi cells), roughly spherical (the distance to the center is the only thing that matters, not its direction) and of similar size and density (a large cluster next to a small one is split in the wrong place, because the objective prefers to cut the large one). Gaussian mixtures (Section 12.7.1) relax the spherical assumption, spectral clustering (Section 12.8) the convexity.

12.4 Evaluating a clustering¶

The objective JJJ cannot be used to compare clusterings with different numbers of groups (Section 12.5), and it says nothing about whether a partition is useful. Two kinds of criteria exist. Internal criteria look only at the data and the partition; external criteria compare the partition with a grouping that is known independently, such as the species of Iris. Both are needed, and neither is a loss in the sense of the previous chapters: there is no unique correct answer to be right about.

12.4.1 Without labels: the silhouette¶

Definition 12.3 (silhouette)

Let d(x,x′)=∥x−x′∥d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\rVertd(x,x′)=∥x−x′∥ and let example iii belong to the cluster CjC_jCj​ with nj≥2n_j\ge2nj​≥2. Let

a(i)=1nj−1∑i′∈Cj, i′≠id(xi,xi′),b(i)=min⁡l≠j1nl∑i′∈Cld(xi,xi′),s(i)=b(i)−a(i)max⁡{a(i),b(i)}∈[−1,1],a(i)=\frac1{n_j-1}\sum_{i'\in C_j,\,i'\ne i}d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_{i'}),\qquad b(i)=\min_{l\ne j}\frac1{n_l}\sum_{i'\in C_l}d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_{i'}),\qquad s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}\in[-1,1],a(i)=nj​−11​i′∈Cj​,i′=i∑​d(xi​,xi′​),b(i)=l=jmin​nl​1​i′∈Cl​∑​d(xi​,xi′​),s(i)=max{a(i),b(i)}b(i)−a(i)​∈[−1,1],
(7)

the mean distance to the other members of its own cluster, the mean distance to the nearest other cluster, and the silhouette of the example (s(i)=0s(i)=0s(i)=0 if nj=1n_j=1nj​=1). The silhouette score of a clustering is the mean of s(i)s(i)s(i) over the examples.

A silhouette near 1 means that the example is much closer to its own cluster than to any other; near 0, that it lies between two clusters; negative, that it is on average closer to another cluster than to its own. The score is computed in O(n2p)O(n^2p)O(n2p) operations. It compares the cohesion of a cluster with its separation from the nearest neighbor cluster, which is why it can compare partitions with different numbers of clusters, which JJJ cannot do. The code computes it from the definition, compares it with scikit-learn and draws the silhouette diagram of Iris for k=2k=2k=2 and k=3k=3k=3: one bar per example, grouped by cluster and sorted inside the cluster.

def silhouette_from_scratch(X, labels):
    D = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - X[None, :, :], axis=2)
    ks = np.unique(labels)
    s = np.zeros(len(X))
    for i in range(len(X)):
        own = labels == labels[i]
        if own.sum() < 2:
            continue
        a = D[i, own].sum() / (own.sum() - 1)
        b = min(D[i, labels == l].mean() for l in ks if l != labels[i])
        s[i] = (b - a) / max(a, b)
    return s


iris_km = {k: KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X_iris) for k in (2, 3)}
for k, m in iris_km.items():
    s = silhouette_from_scratch(X_iris, m.labels_)
    print(f"Iris, k = {k}: silhouette score {s.mean():.4f} (scikit-learn {silhouette_score(X_iris, m.labels_):.4f}, "
          f"largest difference per example {np.abs(s - silhouette_samples(X_iris, m.labels_)).max():.1e}); "
          f"negative silhouettes: {int((s < 0).sum())}; mean per cluster: "
          + ", ".join(f"{s[m.labels_ == j].mean():.3f}" for j in range(k)))


def figure_12_3():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), sharex=True)
    for ax, (k, m) in zip(axes, iris_km.items()):
        s = silhouette_samples(X_iris, m.labels_)
        pos = 0
        for j in range(k):
            sj = np.sort(s[m.labels_ == j])
            ax.barh(np.arange(pos, pos + len(sj)), sj, height=1.0, color=CLUSTER_COLORS[j], edgecolor="none")
            ax.text(-0.05, pos + len(sj) / 2, f"{j}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10)
            pos += len(sj) + 4
        ax.axvline(s.mean(), color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
        ax.set_title(f"k = {k}: silhouette score {s.mean():.3f}")
        ax.set_xlabel("silhouette s(i)")
        ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.grid(False)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("examples, grouped by cluster")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_3()
Iris, k = 2: silhouette score 0.6810 (scikit-learn 0.6810, largest difference per example 2.2e-15); negative silhouettes: 0; mean per cluster: 0.633, 0.770
Iris, k = 3: silhouette score 0.5528 (scikit-learn 0.5528, largest difference per example 4.8e-15); negative silhouettes: 0; mean per cluster: 0.417, 0.798, 0.451

The code agrees with scikit-learn to rounding error (differences of order 10-15 per example). The score is 0.681 for k=2k=2k=2 and 0.553 for k=3k=3k=3, and neither partition has an example with a negative silhouette. The diagrams show where the score comes from. With k=2k=2k=2 the cluster that contains setosa (on average 0.770) is compact and far from the other, and the other one, which contains the 100 flowers of the two large species, averages 0.633. With k=3k=3k=3 setosa keeps its high values (0.798) but the two clusters into which the large species are divided, 0.417 and 0.451, have many flowers with a silhouette near 0: their flowers are about as close to the neighbor cluster as to their own, which is the overlap of versicolor and virginica seen in Figure 12.1. The silhouette therefore prefers two clusters for Iris. That is not an error of the index: at the scale of the whole sample the data really do consist of two groups, a well separated one and a diffuse one; the third group exists at a finer scale and with a much weaker separation. The species were defined by botanists with other information.

12.4.2 With labels: the adjusted Rand index¶

Suppose that a reference partition U\mathcal{U}U of the examples is available (the species, the digits). The agreement between a clustering V={V1,…,Vk}\mathcal{V}=\{V_1,\dots,V_k\}V={V1​,…,Vk​} and U={U1,…,Ur}\mathcal{U}=\{U_1,\dots,U_r\}U={U1​,…,Ur​} cannot be measured by the accuracy, because the cluster labels have no meaning (cluster 0 may be the species 2), and the numbers of groups may differ. The remedy is to count pairs of examples, which do not depend on the names.

Definition 12.4 (Rand index and adjusted Rand index)

Let nij=∣Ui∩Vj∣n_{ij}=\lvert U_i\cap V_j\rvertnij​=∣Ui​∩Vj​∣ be the contingency table, with row sums ai=∣Ui∣a_i=\lvert U_i\rvertai​=∣Ui​∣ and column sums bj=∣Vj∣b_j=\lvert V_j\rvertbj​=∣Vj​∣. A pair of examples is together in a partition if they belong to the same group. The number of pairs together in both partitions is ∑ij(nij2)\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2∑ij​(2nij​​), and the Rand index is the fraction of pairs on which the two partitions agree (together in both or apart in both),

R=(n2)−1[(n2)+2∑ij(nij2)−∑i(ai2)−∑j(bj2)].R=\binom n2^{-1}\Big[\binom n2+2\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2-\sum_i\binom{a_i}2-\sum_j\binom{b_j}2\Big].R=(2n​)−1[(2n​)+2ij∑​(2nij​​)−i∑​(2ai​​)−j∑​(2bj​​)].
(8)

The adjusted Rand index (Hubert and Arabie, 1985) is

ARI=∑ij(nij2)−[∑i(ai2)∑j(bj2)]/(n2)12[∑i(ai2)+∑j(bj2)]−[∑i(ai2)∑j(bj2)]/(n2).\mathrm{ARI}=\frac{\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2-\Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}2\sum_j\binom{b_j}2\Big]\Big/\binom n2}{\frac12\Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}2+\sum_j\binom{b_j}2\Big]-\Big[\sum_i\binom{a_i}2\sum_j\binom{b_j}2\Big]\Big/\binom n2}.ARI=21​[∑i​(2ai​​)+∑j​(2bj​​)]−[∑i​(2ai​​)∑j​(2bj​​)]/(2n​)∑ij​(2nij​​)−[∑i​(2ai​​)∑j​(2bj​​)]/(2n​)​.
(9)
Proposition 12.7 (properties of the ARI)

(a) The ARI does not change when the groups of either partition are renamed. (b) ARI≤1\mathrm{ARI}\le1ARI≤1, with equality if and only if the two partitions are equal. (c) If the two partitions are fixed and the elements of one of them are permuted uniformly at random (the permutation model, in which the group sizes aia_iai​ and bjb_jbj​ are fixed), then E[∑ij(nij2)]=∑i(ai2)∑j(bj2)/(n2)\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2\big]=\sum_i\binom{a_i}2\sum_j\binom{b_j}2/\binom n2E[∑ij​(2nij​​)]=∑i​(2ai​​)∑j​(2bj​​)/(2n​), so that the numerator of the ARI has expectation 0. The ARI of a partition unrelated to the reference is thus close to 0 (and can be slightly negative), whatever the numbers of groups.

Proof. (a) The formula uses only the numbers nijn_{ij}nij​, aia_iai​, bjb_jbj​, which are permuted by a renaming. (c) ∑ij(nij2)\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2∑ij​(2nij​​) counts the pairs together in both partitions. Take one of the ∑i(ai2)\sum_i\binom{a_i}2∑i​(2ai​​) pairs together in U\mathcal{U}U; under a random permutation of the examples of V\mathcal{V}V the two examples occupy two positions chosen uniformly among all (n2)\binom n2(2n​) pairs of positions, and the probability that the pair is together in V\mathcal{V}V is ∑j(bj2)/(n2)\sum_j\binom{b_j}2/\binom n2∑j​(2bj​​)/(2n​); sum over the pairs. (b) Since nij≤ain_{ij}\le a_inij​≤ai​ and nij≤bjn_{ij}\le b_jnij​≤bj​, every pair counted in ∑ij(nij2)\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2∑ij​(2nij​​) is counted in ∑i(ai2)\sum_i\binom{a_i}2∑i​(2ai​​) and in ∑j(bj2)\sum_j\binom{b_j}2∑j​(2bj​​), so ∑ij(nij2)≤min⁡{∑i(ai2),∑j(bj2)}≤12[⋯+⋯ ]\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2\le\min\{\sum_i\binom{a_i}2,\sum_j\binom{b_j}2\}\le\frac12[\cdots+\cdots]∑ij​(2nij​​)≤min{∑i​(2ai​​),∑j​(2bj​​)}≤21​[⋯+⋯], which makes the numerator at most the denominator. Equality forces the two sums to be equal to ∑ij(nij2)\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}2∑ij​(2nij​​): every pair together in one partition is together in the other, which means that the partitions are equal. ■\blacksquare■

The adjustment is the point of the definition. The Rand index of two unrelated partitions is far from 0 (most pairs are apart in both), and the normalized mutual information NMI=I(U;V)/12[H(U)+H(V)]\mathrm{NMI}=I(\mathcal{U};\mathcal{V})\big/\tfrac12[H(\mathcal{U})+H(\mathcal{V})]NMI=I(U;V)/21​[H(U)+H(V)], with III the mutual information and HHH the entropy of the group-membership distributions, also grows when the number of groups grows, even for random labels. The code computes the ARI from the contingency table, and the values obtained by random labels.

def ari_from_scratch(u, v):
    table = pd.crosstab(np.asarray(u), np.asarray(v)).to_numpy()
    c2 = lambda m: m * (m - 1) / 2
    sum_ij, sum_a, sum_b = c2(table).sum(), c2(table.sum(1)).sum(), c2(table.sum(0)).sum()
    expected = sum_a * sum_b / c2(table.sum())
    return float((sum_ij - expected) / (0.5 * (sum_a + sum_b) - expected))

The contingency table reads as the picture of Figure 12.1: setosa is entirely in one cluster, and the other two clusters share versicolor and virginica: cluster 0 holds 48 versicolor and 14 virginica flowers, cluster 2 holds 36 virginica and 2 versicolor. The ARI is 0.7302; our code and scikit-learn give the same value to six decimals, and renaming the clusters does not change it. The NMI of the same partition is 0.7582, a different number on a different scale: the two scores cannot be compared with each other.

The last table is the reason for the adjustment. Random labels, unrelated to the digits, have ARI equal to 0 to the fourth decimal for every number of groups from 3 to 200, as Proposition 12.7(c) says. The NMI of the same random labels grows with the number of groups, from 0.003 with 3 groups to 0.151 with 200, which is a score of 0.15 for pure noise: a clustering with many small groups can raise its NMI without containing any information. For this reason the ARI is the main external score of the chapter, and the NMI is reported only as a second opinion, in comparisons between partitions with the same number of clusters.

An external score measures agreement with one grouping of the data. A low ARI does not prove a bad clustering (the groups of the data may be real and different from the labels: the two groups of Section 12.5 on Iris are an example), and a high ARI does not prove that the partition is the only reasonable one. We use the ARI throughout because it is what the reader can check, and we say each time that the labels played no role in the choice of the method or the parameters.

12.5 Choosing the number of clusters¶

12.5.1 The objective cannot do it¶

In a supervised problem the number of parameters (the depth of a tree, the penalty of a ridge) is chosen by looking at an error on data that were not used for fitting (Chapter 5). For clustering the natural analogue fails, for the same reason that the training error of Chapter 3 always favors the richest model.

Proposition 12.8 (JJJ decreases with kkk)

Let J∗(k)=min⁡CSSW(C)J^\ast(k)=\min_{\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{SS}_W(\mathcal{C})J∗(k)=minC​SSW​(C) be the minimum of the within-cluster scatter over the partitions into kkk groups. Then J∗(1)=SSTJ^\ast(1)=\mathrm{SS}_TJ∗(1)=SST​, J∗(k+1)≤J∗(k)J^\ast(k+1)\le J^\ast(k)J∗(k+1)≤J∗(k) for k<nk<nk<n, and J∗(n)=0J^\ast(n)=0J∗(n)=0.

Proof. Take an optimal partition into k<nk<nk<n groups. One of its groups has at least two examples; moving one of them to a group of its own does not increase the scatter by (12.2) (splitting never increases it), and produces a partition into k+1k+1k+1 groups. The last statements are clear. ■\blacksquare■

The same holds for the objective evaluated on held-out examples when the centers are those fitted on the training examples: the held-out distortion decreases with kkk for a long time, as we show below, because more centers are always nearer to a new point. So no validation set can pick kkk by the minimum of JJJ; four other families of criteria are in use.

  1. The elbow. Plot J∗(k)J^\ast(k)J∗(k) against kkk and look for a bend after which the decrease is small. The idea is that the decrease is large while a new center explains a real group and small when it only splits a group in two (Proposition 12.2(b) says by how much, nAnBnA+nB∥μA−μB∥2\frac{n_An_B}{n_A+n_B}\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2nA​+nB​nA​nB​​∥μA​−μB​∥2). There is no rule, and the bend is often not there.

  2. The silhouette. Choose the kkk that maximizes the mean silhouette (Section 12.4.1).

  3. The gap statistic (Tibshirani, Walther and Hastie, 2001). Compare log⁡J∗(k)\log J^\ast(k)logJ∗(k) with its expectation for data with no cluster structure, drawn uniformly in the bounding box of the data: Gap(k)=1B∑b=1Blog⁡Jb∗(k)−log⁡J∗(k)\mathrm{Gap}(k)=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B\log J^\ast_b(k)-\log J^\ast(k)Gap(k)=B1​∑b=1B​logJb∗​(k)−logJ∗(k), with Jb∗J^\ast_bJb∗​ computed on BBB reference data sets. Choose the smallest kkk such that Gap(k)≥Gap(k+1)−sk+1\mathrm{Gap}(k)\ge\mathrm{Gap}(k+1)-s_{k+1}Gap(k)≥Gap(k+1)−sk+1​, where sks_{k}sk​ is the standard deviation of log⁡Jb∗(k)\log J^\ast_b(k)logJb∗​(k) times 1+1/B\sqrt{1+1/B}1+1/B​.

  4. Stability (Ben-Hur, Elisseeff and Guyon, 2002; Lange, Roth, Braun and Buhmann, 2004). If the data really have kkk groups, two clusterings computed from two independent samples should agree; if kkk is too large, the algorithm has to cut a group in two somewhere and cuts it in a different place each time. We draw two disjoint halves of the data, cluster each with kkk-means, assign all the examples to the nearest center of each of the two solutions, and measure the ARI between the two assignments; the average over repeated random halves is the stability of kkk. This is the instability of trees of Section 11.5.5, used as a criterion: a partition that changes a lot when a few examples change is not determined by the data.

The code computes the four quantities for k=1,…,8k=1,\dots,8k=1,…,8 on Iris and Wine and k=1,…,15k=1,\dots,15k=1,…,15 on Digits. The numbers of classes (3, 3, 10) are used only to mark the plot.

def gap_statistic(X, ks, B=20, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lo, hi = X.min(axis=0), X.max(axis=0)
    log_j = np.array([np.log(KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X).inertia_) for k in ks])
    ref = np.array([[np.log(KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=SEED).fit(rng.uniform(lo, hi, X.shape)).inertia_) for k in ks] for _ in range(B)])
    gap, s = ref.mean(axis=0) - log_j, ref.std(axis=0) * np.sqrt(1 + 1 / B)
    chosen = next((ks[i] for i in range(len(ks) - 1) if gap[i] >= gap[i + 1] - s[i + 1]), None)
    return gap, s, chosen


def stability(X, k, reps=15, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        perm = rng.permutation(len(X))
        half = len(X) // 2
        m1 = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=int(rng.integers(10 ** 9))).fit(X[perm[:half]])
        m2 = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=int(rng.integers(10 ** 9))).fit(X[perm[half:2 * half]])
        out.append(adjusted_rand_score(m1.predict(X), m2.predict(X)))
    return np.array(out)


k_study = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for name, kmax in [("Iris", 8), ("Wine", 8), ("Digits", 15)]:

    ks = list(range(1, kmax + 1))
    models = {k: KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X) for k in ks}
    gap, s_gap, k_gap = gap_statistic(X, ks)
    stab = {k: stability(X, k) for k in ks if k >= 2}
    k_study[name] = {"ks": ks, "J": np.array([models[k].inertia_ for k in ks]),
                     "sil": np.array([np.nan] + [silhouette_score(X, models[k].labels_) for k in ks[1:]]),
                     "gap": gap, "gap_s": s_gap, "k_gap": k_gap,
                     "stab": np.array([np.nan] + [stab[k].mean() for k in ks[1:]]), "stab_sd": np.array([np.nan] + [stab[k].std(ddof=1) for k in ks[1:]]),
                     "ari": np.array([adjusted_rand_score(y, models[k].labels_) for k in ks])}

The four criteria, applied to the same partitions, do not give one answer.

Iris. The silhouette (0.681 at k=2k=2k=2 against 0.553 at k=3k=3k=3) and the stability (0.977 against 0.841) choose k=2k=2k=2. The elbow is ambiguous: 78%78\%78% of the total scatter disappears with the second center and a further 11%11\%11% with the third, and then about 3%3\%3% or less with each. The gap statistic gives no answer: the rule finds no k≤8k\le8k≤8 at which the curve stops growing, and the gap grows steadily from 0.08 to 1.82. The reason is the choice of the reference distribution: Iris has strongly correlated features, so it looks clustered compared with data uniform in the bounding box at every kkk (Tibshirani et al. proposed to draw the reference in a box aligned with the principal components for this reason). The ARI with the species, which was not used by any criterion, is highest at k=3k=3k=3 (0.730), and 0.540 at k=2k=2k=2. The criteria are not wrong and the species are not wrong: they answer two different questions, “how many groups does the geometry show?” and “how many species did the botanists distinguish?”.

Wine. Here the criteria agree: the silhouette (0.285) and the stability (0.883, standard deviation 0.064) are largest at k=3k=3k=3, the elbow has its bend there (J/SSTJ/\mathrm{SS}_TJ/SST​ falls from 0.717 to 0.552 and then more slowly), and the ARI with the cultivars is largest at 3 (0.897). The gap rule chooses 4, not 3, because the gap at k=3k=3k=3 (1.191) is smaller than the gap at k=4k=4k=4 (1.231) minus its standard error (0.015). The agreement is moderate: a silhouette of 0.285 is in the range that Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990) describe as weak structure, and the margin over k=2k=2k=2 and k=4k=4k=4 is 0.025.

Digits. The criteria are even less decisive. JJJ decreases smoothly and has no elbow. The silhouette rises to a maximum at k=9k=9k=9 (0.189) and stays within 0.007 of it up to k=15k=15k=15, a plateau rather than a peak. The stability is largest at 9 (0.826), but the value for 10 (0.805) is within one standard deviation (0.108). The gap rule gives no answer, for the reason given for Iris. And the ARI with the digit labels is highest at k=11k=11k=11 and 13 (0.726), against 0.667 at k=10k=10k=10. No criterion finds the ten classes, and one must ask whether it should: kkk-means partitions the pixel space by Euclidean distance, and the ten digits are not necessarily ten compact groups in that space, since handwriting varies a great deal inside one digit.

def figure_12_4():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(14, 8.4))
    titles = ["J* (k) / SS_T (elbow)", "silhouette score", "gap statistic", "stability (ARI of two halves)"]
    for row, (name, r) in enumerate(k_study.items()):
        ks = np.array(r["ks"])
        n_true = len(np.unique(datasets[name][1]))
        series = [(r["J"] / r["J"][0], None), (r["sil"], None), (r["gap"], r["gap_s"]), (r["stab"], r["stab_sd"])]
        for col, (ax, (v, err)) in enumerate(zip(axes[row], series)):
            ax.errorbar(ks, v, yerr=err, color=BLUE, marker="o", markersize=5, linewidth=1.6, capsize=2)
            ax.axvline(n_true, color=VERMILION, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
            if row == 0:
                ax.set_title(titles[col])
            if col == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(name)
            if row == 2:
                ax.set_xlabel("number of clusters k")
            ax.set_xticks(ks if len(ks) <= 8 else ks[::2])
    fig.suptitle("Four criteria for the number of clusters (dotted line: the number of classes, not used by any criterion)", y=1.0)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_4()

Figure 12.4 shows the same numbers. In each row the dotted line marks the number of classes. For Iris the silhouette and the stability decrease from k=2k=2k=2 on, with the stability bars (one standard deviation over 15 pairs of halves) wide for k≥3k\ge3k≥3. For Wine the silhouette and the stability have a peak at 3, the only case in which the peak is visible in both, and the gap curve has a corner there. For Digits the curves are smooth, the peak of the silhouette is a shoulder, and the dotted line at 10 does not coincide with anything. The conclusion is that the number of clusters is not a property of the data alone: it depends on the criterion, the scale of the structure sought and the purpose. In practice one looks at several criteria, at the partitions themselves, and asks which number is useful for what the clusters will be used for (Section 12.9 gives an example in which a deliberately larger kkk is the right choice).

12.5.2 A validation set does not help either¶

To see the claim about held-out data, we split Digits at random into 900 examples for fitting and 897 held out, fit kkk-means on the first part and compute the mean squared distance of the held-out examples to their nearest center.

perm = np.random.default_rng(SEED).permutation(len(X_dig))
fit_idx, held_idx = perm[:900], perm[900:]
rows = []
for k in [2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400]:
    m = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=SEED).fit(X_dig[fit_idx])
    held = ((X_dig[held_idx] - m.cluster_centers_[m.predict(X_dig[held_idx])]) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
    rows.append({"k": k, "mean distortion, fitting examples": m.inertia_ / len(fit_idx), "mean distortion, held-out examples": held})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
  k  mean distortion, fitting examples  mean distortion, held-out examples
  2                              4.196                               4.214
  5                              3.289                               3.293
 10                              2.526                               2.580
 20                              2.051                               2.151
 50                              1.517                               1.785
100                              1.154                               1.603
200                              0.797                               1.454
400                              0.413                               1.380

The distortion of the held-out examples decreases at every step, from 4.214 with 2 centers to 1.380 with 400, so that it never signals “enough”. Overfitting shows up as a gap that widens: the ratio of the held-out to the fitting distortion is 1.00 with 2 centers and then 1.02, 1.05, 1.18, 1.39, 1.82 and 3.34 with 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 400 (the last is two fitting examples per center). The curve is flattening, which is the information that the elbow looks for, and it has the same ambiguity. A validation set measures how well the codebook describes new data, which is the right question for quantization (Section 12.6), but it does not tell us how many groups the data have.

12.6 Vector quantization: kkk-means as compression¶

12.6.1 Quantizers, rate and distortion¶

So far kkk-means found groups. The same algorithm answers a different question from communications engineering: how to represent a vector x∈Rp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^px∈Rp with a few bits, losing as little as possible. A vector quantizer with kkk codewords consists of a codebook μ1,…,μk∈Rp\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k\in\mathbb{R}^pμ1​,…,μk​∈Rp and an encoder that sends x\mathbf{x}x to the index j(x)j(\mathbf{x})j(x) of a codeword; the decoder reconstructs x^=μj(x)\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\boldsymbol\mu_{j(\mathbf{x})}x^=μj(x)​. Storing the index takes log⁡2k\log_2klog2​k bits (the rate) in place of the ppp numbers of x\mathbf{x}x, and the price is the distortion D=E∥X−X^∥2D=\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{X}-\hat{\mathbf{X}}\rVert^2D=E∥X−X^∥2. On a sample, the distortion of the quantizer is J/nJ/nJ/n, with JJJ the kkk-means objective (12.3): kkk-means is the design of an optimal quantizer for the empirical distribution, and the two conditions of Proposition 12.3 are the necessary conditions of Lloyd (1957, published 1982) and Max (1960) for scalars, extended to vectors by Linde, Buzo and Gray (1980): the best encoder for a codebook sends each vector to its nearest codeword, and the best codeword for an encoder is the mean of the vectors sent to it.

How does the best achievable distortion depend on the rate? For a source with a density the answer is classical, and we state it without proof.

Theorem 12.9 (high-resolution quantization; Zador, 1964, stated without proof)

Let X∈Rp\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^pX∈Rp have a density fff with a finite moment of order slightly above 2, and let D∗(k)D^\ast(k)D∗(k) be the smallest distortion of a quantizer with kkk codewords. Then, as k→∞k\to\inftyk→∞,

D∗(k)  ∼  cp ∥f∥p/(p+2)  k−2/p,D^\ast(k)\;\sim\;c_p\,\lVert f\rVert_{p/(p+2)}\;k^{-2/p},D∗(k)∼cp​∥f∥p/(p+2)​k−2/p,
(10)

where cpc_pcp​ depends only on the dimension and ∥f∥p/(p+2)=(∫fp/(p+2))(p+2)/p\lVert f\rVert_{p/(p+2)}=\big(\int f^{p/(p+2)}\big)^{(p+2)/p}∥f∥p/(p+2)​=(∫fp/(p+2))(p+2)/p.

The exponent is what matters: on a log–log plot the distortion falls along a line of slope −2/p-2/p−2/p, so that doubling the number of codewords, one more bit, divides the distortion by 22/p2^{2/p}22/p (by 4, that is 6 dB, in dimension 1; by only 22/64≈1.022^{2/64}\approx1.0222/64≈1.02 in dimension 64). The theorem is about data that fill a ppp-dimensional region. When the data lie near a lower-dimensional set, the slope measured on a sample is that of the lower dimension, and deff=−2/sloped_{\text{eff}}=-2/\text{slope}deff​=−2/slope is an effective dimension of the data, in the sense of Section 4.7.3.

12.6.2 Quantizing the colors of a photograph¶

The data are the 427×640=273,280427\times640=273{,}280427×640=273,280 pixels of the photograph china.jpg that ships with scikit-learn (a real photograph, Creative Commons licensed; see the data sources). Each pixel is a point of [0,1]3[0,1]^3[0,1]3 (red, green, blue). We fit the codebook on a random subsample of 20,00020{,}00020,000 pixels, which is what one does with large images, and encode all the pixels with it. As a baseline we use the uniform quantizer that rounds each channel to LLL equally spaced levels, with L3L^3L3 colors.

img = load_sample_image("china.jpg")
pix = img.reshape(-1, 3).astype(float) / 255
sub = pix[np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(len(pix), 20000, replace=False)]
print(f"image {img.shape[1]} x {img.shape[0]} pixels = {len(pix):,} points of [0, 1]^3, codebook fitted on {len(sub):,} of them")


def quantization_error(P, recon):
    mse = float(((P - recon) ** 2).mean())                 # mean squared error per channel
    return mse, 10 * np.log10(1 / mse)                     # and the peak signal-to-noise ratio in dB


vq_models, rows = {}, []
for k in [2, 4, 8, 16, 27, 32, 64, 128, 216, 256]:
    vq_models[k] = KMeans(k, n_init=1, random_state=SEED).fit(sub)
    mse, psnr = quantization_error(pix, vq_models[k].cluster_centers_[vq_models[k].predict(pix)])
    row = {"k": k, "bits per pixel": np.log2(k), "compression (24 bits / rate)": 24 / np.log2(k), "MSE": mse, "PSNR (dB)": psnr}
    L = round(k ** (1 / 3))
    if L ** 3 == k:                                          # uniform per-channel baseline with the same number of colors
        row["uniform quantizer MSE, same k"] = quantization_error(pix, np.round(pix * (L - 1)) / (L - 1))[0]
    rows.append(row)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.5f}" if v < 0.1 else f"{v:.2f}"))

used = {L ** 3: len(np.unique(np.round(pix * (L - 1)).astype(int), axis=0)) for L in (2, 3, 4, 6)}
print("\ncolors of the uniform grid that the photograph actually uses:", ", ".join(f"{u} of {k}" for k, u in used.items()))

ks_img = np.array([k for k in vq_models if k >= 16])
mse_img = np.array([quantization_error(pix, vq_models[k].cluster_centers_[vq_models[k].predict(pix)])[0] for k in ks_img])
slope_img = np.polyfit(np.log(ks_img), np.log(mse_img), 1)[0]
print(f"\nlog-log slope of the distortion for k >= 16: {slope_img:.3f}; effective dimension -2/slope = {-2 / slope_img:.2f} (the pixels live in 3 dimensions)")

  4            2.00                         12.00 0.00702      21.54                            NaN

128            7.00                          3.43 0.00037      34.33                            NaN
216            7.75                          3.09 0.00026      35.88                        0.00315

log-log slope of the distortion for k >= 16: -0.734; effective dimension -2/slope = 2.73 (the pixels live in 3 dimensions)

The distortion falls steadily with the number of colors, and so does the visual error: with k=16k=16k=16 colors (4 bits per pixel instead of 24, a compression of 6:16:16:1) the PSNR is 27.4 dB, with 256 colors (8 bits, 3:13:13:1) it is 36.4 dB. (The sizes ignore the codebook, which has 256 colors of 24 bits, under a thousand bytes, against 273,280273{,}280273,280 indices.) A codebook fitted to the colors of this image is much better than a fixed grid: with 8 and with 27 colors the mean squared error of kkk-means is about 16 times smaller than that of the uniform quantizer (0.0033 against 0.0539, and 0.0012 against 0.0188), with 64 colors 15 times, and with 216 colors 12 times (0.00026 against 0.00315). The reason is visible in the last line of the output: the uniform grid wastes colors on regions of the color cube where this photograph has no pixel (it uses 17 of the 27 grid colors, 33 of 64 and 82 of 216), and the codebook puts every codeword where the pixels are.

The slope of the log-log curve of the distortion for k≥16k\ge16k≥16 is -0.734, which Theorem 12.9 turns into an effective dimension −2/slope=2.73-2/\text{slope}=2.73−2/slope=2.73 for pixels that live in 3 dimensions: the estimate is consistent with the colors of a natural image occupying a region of the color cube that is slightly thinner than the cube. The measure should not be over-read, since it comes from a range of kkk that spans little more than one decade and the asymptotic regime of the theorem is far away. Figure 12.5 shows the image with 4, 16 and 64 colors. With 4 colors the sky and the water merge, and the red of the tower is lost; with 16 the reds and greens are back, but the smooth sky breaks into visible bands (false contours), which are the price of too few codewords for a region where the colors change slowly; with 64 colors the image is close to the original and only slight banding remains in the sky.

def figure_12_5():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.1))
    panels = [("original image", img)] + [(f"k = {k} colors ({int(np.log2(k))} bits)", (vq_models[k].cluster_centers_[vq_models[k].predict(pix)].reshape(img.shape) * 255).round().astype(np.uint8))
                                          for k in (4, 16, 64)]
    for ax, (title, im) in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.imshow(im)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_5()

12.6.3 Digits as a codebook of images¶

On Digits the points are 64-dimensional, and the theorem predicts a distortion that falls very slowly with kkk if the images filled their space. We fit codebooks of 2 to 200 images and look at the rate–distortion curve and at the reconstructions.

dig_vq, rows = {}, []
for k in [2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200]:
    dig_vq[k] = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=SEED).fit(X_dig)
    rows.append({"k": k, "bits per image": np.log2(k), "MSE per pixel": dig_vq[k].inertia_ / X_dig.size,
                 "ARI with the digits": adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, dig_vq[k].labels_)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
ks_dig = np.array([k for k in dig_vq if k >= 10])
slope_dig = np.polyfit(np.log(ks_dig), np.log([dig_vq[k].inertia_ / X_dig.size for k in ks_dig]), 1)[0]
print(f"\nlog-log slope for k >= 10: {slope_dig:.3f}; effective dimension -2/slope = {-2 / slope_dig:.1f} (the images have 64 pixels)")
  k  bits per image  MSE per pixel  ARI with the digits
  2          1.0000         0.0650               0.1381
  5          2.3219         0.0516               0.3392
 10          3.3219         0.0396               0.6669
 20          4.3219         0.0322               0.6259
