200          7.6439         0.0150               0.0936

log-log slope for k >= 10: -0.319; effective dimension -2/slope = 6.3 (the images have 64 pixels)

Ten codewords, 3.3 bits per image, reduce the distortion to 54%54\%54% of the total variance (J/SST=0.540J/\mathrm{SS}_T=0.540J/SST​=0.540); 200 codewords reduce it to 0.0150 per pixel, against 0.0733 for the mean image. The log-log slope for k≥10k\ge10k≥10 is -0.319, which gives an effective dimension of 6.3. For a cloud that filled the 64-dimensional space the slope would be −2/64=−0.031-2/64=-0.031−2/64=−0.031, ten times flatter: the images are much more compressible than their dimension would suggest, which is the observation of Section 4.7.3 seen from another side. The number 6.3 is lower than the ten to twenty components found there, and it should not be taken as a measurement of the dimension: with 1797 images and at most 200 codewords we are far from the asymptotic regime of the theorem (about nine images per codeword at k=200k=200k=200), and the distortion is measured on the images used for fitting, which flatters large codebooks.

The last column is a reminder that the quantizer and the clustering are different uses of one algorithm. The ARI with the digit labels is highest at k=10k=10k=10 (0.667) and falls as the codebook grows (0.333 with 50 codewords, 0.094 with 200), although the distortion keeps decreasing: a partition into 200 small groups does not match a partition into ten classes, even when each of the small groups is pure. The distortion measures how well the images are represented, the ARI how well the partition reproduces the ten classes; neither is a substitute for the other.

def figure_12_6():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
    ax = axes[0]
    ks_all = np.array(sorted(vq_models))
    mse_all = np.array([quantization_error(pix, vq_models[k].cluster_centers_[vq_models[k].predict(pix)])[0] for k in ks_all])
    ax.loglog(ks_all, mse_all, "o-", color=BLUE, label="k-means codebook")
    uni_k = [8, 27, 64, 216]
    uni = [quantization_error(pix, np.round(pix * (round(k ** (1 / 3)) - 1)) / (round(k ** (1 / 3)) - 1))[0] for k in uni_k]
    ax.loglog(uni_k, uni, "s--", color=ORANGE, label="uniform quantizer (L³ colors)")
    c = np.polyfit(np.log(ks_img), np.log(mse_img), 1)
    ax.loglog(ks_img, np.exp(np.polyval(c, np.log(ks_img))), ":", color="black", label=f"slope {slope_img:.2f} (d_eff = {-2 / slope_img:.1f})")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of codewords k", ylabel="MSE per channel", title="(a) photograph, 3 dimensions")
    ax.set_xticks([2, 8, 32, 128, 512], ["2", "8", "32", "128", "512"])
    ax.minorticks_off()
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax = axes[1]
    ks_d = np.array(sorted(dig_vq))
    mse_d = np.array([dig_vq[k].inertia_ / X_dig.size for k in ks_d])
    ax.loglog(ks_d, mse_d, "o-", color=GREEN, label="k-means codebook")
    c = np.polyfit(np.log(ks_dig), np.log([dig_vq[k].inertia_ / X_dig.size for k in ks_dig]), 1)
    ax.loglog(ks_dig, np.exp(np.polyval(c, np.log(ks_dig))), ":", color="black", label=f"slope {slope_dig:.2f} (d_eff = {-2 / slope_dig:.1f})")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of codewords k", ylabel="MSE per pixel", title="(b) Digits, 64 dimensions")
    ax.set_xticks([2, 10, 50, 200], ["2", "10", "50", "200"])
    ax.set_yticks([0.015, 0.025, 0.04, 0.065], ["0.015", "0.025", "0.04", "0.065"])
    ax.minorticks_off()
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def figure_12_7():
    ks_show = [10, 50, 200]
    first = [int(np.where(y_dig == d)[0][0]) for d in range(10)]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2 + len(ks_show), 10, figsize=(10, 5.6))
    rows_img = [("codebook\nk = 10", dig_vq[10].cluster_centers_), ("original", X_dig[first])] + \
               [(f"k = {k}", dig_vq[k].cluster_centers_[dig_vq[k].predict(X_dig[first])]) for k in ks_show]
    for r, (label, imgs) in enumerate(rows_img):
        for c in range(10):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            ax.imshow(imgs[c].reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1)
            ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
            for sp_ in ax.spines.values():
                sp_.set_visible(False)
        axes[r, 0].set_ylabel(label, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_7()

Figure 12.6 shows the rate–distortion curves. In (a) the points of the photograph follow the line closely for k≥16k\ge16k≥16, and the uniform quantizer stays above the codebook at every size shown. In (b) the Digits curve is also a straight line in these coordinates, much steeper than a 64-dimensional cloud would allow.

Figure 12.7 shows what the codewords look like. The first row is the codebook with k=10k=10k=10: blurred images that average the examples of a group, several of which resemble a digit. Below, the first example of each digit and its reconstruction by codebooks of 10, 50 and 200 images. With 10 codewords the reconstruction of the 0, the 3, the 4, the 6, the 7 and the 9 is recognizable, whereas the examples of the 1, the 2 and the 8 are replaced by smudged vertical shapes and the 5 by a codeword that resembles a 9. With 50 codewords most of the images become readable. The example of the digit 5 is still reconstructed by a 9-like codeword even with 200: the encoder minimizes the distance in pixels, not the readability, and for a thick 5 the nearest codeword in pixels can be a 9.

Vector quantization is also the reason why kkk-means is used as a preprocessing step: replacing each example by the index of its codeword (or by its distances to the codewords, as in Section 12.9.3) is a data-driven discretization of the feature space. We use that in a moment; first we leave the Euclidean, convex clusters behind.

12.7 Beyond spheres: Gaussian mixtures and hierarchical clustering¶

12.7.1 Gaussian mixtures and the EM algorithm¶

kkk-means describes a cluster by its center only. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) gives each cluster a center, a covariance matrix and a weight, and treats the data as drawn from a probability density: first a hidden label z∈{1,…,k}z\in\{1,\dots,k\}z∈{1,…,k} is drawn with probabilities π1,…,πk\pi_1,\dots,\pi_kπ1​,…,πk​, then x∼N(μz,Σz)\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_z,\boldsymbol\Sigma_z)x∼N(μz​,Σz​). The density of x\mathbf{x}x is the mixture p(x)=∑j=1kπj N(x;μj,Σj)p(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{j=1}^k\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)p(x)=∑j=1k​πj​N(x;μj​,Σj​), and the parameters θ=(πj,μj,Σj)j\theta=(\pi_j,\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)_jθ=(πj​,μj​,Σj​)j​ are fitted by maximum likelihood (Chapter 2),

ℓ(θ)=∑i=1nlog⁡∑j=1kπj N(xi;μj,Σj).\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\sum_{j=1}^k\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j).ℓ(θ)=i=1∑n​logj=1∑k​πj​N(xi​;μj​,Σj​).
(11)

The logarithm of a sum has no closed-form maximizer. If the labels ziz_izi​ were known the problem would split into kkk ordinary Gaussian fits, and the EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977) exploits this by alternating between guessing the labels and fitting. The guess is the posterior probability of the component jjj for the example iii, the responsibility

rij=Pr⁡(zi=j∣xi)=πj N(xi;μj,Σj)∑lπl N(xi;μl,Σl)(12.4)r_{ij}=\Pr(z_i=j\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\frac{\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)}{\sum_{l}\pi_l\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_l,\boldsymbol\Sigma_l)}\tag{12.4}rij​=Pr(zi​=j∣xi​)=∑l​πl​N(xi​;μl​,Σl​)πj​N(xi​;μj​,Σj​)​(12.4)
(12)

(Bayes’ rule, Chapter 2), a soft assignment: the example belongs to every cluster, with weights that sum to one.

Given responsibilities rijr_{ij}rij​, let Nj=∑irijN_j=\sum_ir_{ij}Nj​=∑i​rij​. The parameters that maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood Q=∑i,jrij[log⁡πj+log⁡N(xi;μj,Σj)]Q=\sum_{i,j}r_{ij}\big[\log\pi_j+\log\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)\big]Q=∑i,j​rij​[logπj​+logN(xi​;μj​,Σj​)] are

Proof. QQQ separates into a term in π\piπ and one term for each (μj,Σj)(\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)(μj​,Σj​). The first, ∑jNjlog⁡πj\sum_jN_j\log\pi_j∑j​Nj​logπj​ with ∑jπj=1\sum_j\pi_j=1∑j​πj​=1, is maximized by πj=Nj/n\pi_j=N_j/nπj​=Nj​/n (a Lagrange multiplier gives Nj/πj=constN_j/\pi_j=\text{const}Nj​/πj​=const). The second is the log-likelihood of a Gaussian sample in which example iii has weight rijr_{ij}rij​, whose maximizers are the weighted mean and the weighted covariance, as in the unweighted case of Chapter 2. ■\blacksquare■

Theorem 12.11 (EM never decreases the likelihood)

Let θt+1\theta^{t+1}θt+1 be obtained from θt\theta^tθt by computing the responsibilities (12.4) at θt\theta^tθt (E-step) and then the parameters (12.5) (M-step). Then ℓ(θt+1)≥ℓ(θt)\ell(\theta^{t+1})\ge\ell(\theta^t)ℓ(θt+1)≥ℓ(θt).

Proof. For any probabilities qijq_{ij}qij​ over jjj with ∑jqij=1\sum_jq_{ij}=1∑j​qij​=1, Jensen’s inequality for the concave logarithm gives

ℓ(θ)=∑ilog⁡∑jqijπjN(xi;μj,Σj)qij  ≥  ∑i,jqijlog⁡πjN(xi;μj,Σj)qij=:F(q,θ),\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log\sum_jq_{ij}\frac{\pi_j\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)}{q_{ij}}\;\ge\;\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}\log\frac{\pi_j\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)}{q_{ij}}=:F(q,\theta),ℓ(θ)=i∑​logj∑​qij​qij​πj​N(xi​;μj​,Σj​)​≥i,j∑​qij​logqij​πj​N(xi​;μj​,Σj​)​=:F(q,θ),
(14)

with equality when the ratio inside the logarithm does not depend on jjj, that is when qijq_{ij}qij​ is the posterior (12.4). The E-step takes q=r(θt)q=r(\theta^t)q=r(θt), so F(q,θt)=ℓ(θt)F(q,\theta^t)=\ell(\theta^t)F(q,θt)=ℓ(θt). The M-step maximizes F(q,⋅)F(q,\cdot)F(q,⋅) over θ\thetaθ (the term −∑qlog⁡q-\sum q\log q−∑qlogq does not depend on θ\thetaθ, and the rest is QQQ of Proposition 12.10), so F(q,θt+1)≥F(q,θt)F(q,\theta^{t+1})\ge F(q,\theta^t)F(q,θt+1)≥F(q,θt). Therefore ℓ(θt+1)≥F(q,θt+1)≥F(q,θt)=ℓ(θt)\ell(\theta^{t+1})\ge F(q,\theta^{t+1})\ge F(q,\theta^t)=\ell(\theta^t)ℓ(θt+1)≥F(q,θt+1)≥F(q,θt)=ℓ(θt). ■\blacksquare■

The likelihood increases at every iteration and, being bounded for covariances kept away from singular matrices, converges; the limit is a stationary point, in general a local maximum, so that the initialization matters here too (scikit-learn starts from a kkk-means partition). The next result connects the two algorithms of the chapter.

Proposition 12.12 (kkk-means is the limit of a mixture with vanishing variance)

Consider the mixture with equal weights πj=1/k\pi_j=1/kπj​=1/k and covariances Σj=σ2I\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\sigma^2\mathbf{I}Σj​=σ2I, with the same σ2\sigma^2σ2 for all the components. As σ2→0\sigma^2\to0σ2→0, the responsibility rijr_{ij}rij​ tends to 1 if μj\boldsymbol\mu_jμj​ is the unique nearest center of xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​ and to 0 otherwise, and the M-step for the centers becomes the update step of Lloyd’s algorithm.

Proof. Here rij∝exp⁡(−∥xi−μj∥2/2σ2)r_{ij}\propto\exp(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)rij​∝exp(−∥xi​−μj​∥2/2σ2). Dividing numerator and denominator by the term of the nearest center j∗j^\astj∗, every other term becomes exp⁡(−(∥xi−μl∥2−∥xi−μj∗∥2)/2σ2)→0\exp\big(-(\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_l\rVert^2-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_{j^\ast}\rVert^2)/2\sigma^2\big)\to0exp(−(∥xi​−μl​∥2−∥xi​−μj∗​∥2)/2σ2)→0. With hard responsibilities, μj\boldsymbol\mu_jμj​ in (12.5) is the mean of the examples assigned to it. ■\blacksquare■

So kkk-means is “hard EM for equal spherical components”, and the mixture adds three things: soft assignments, a covariance per component (clusters that are elongated or tilted), and a likelihood, which allows model comparison. The covariance can be restricted to save parameters: spherical (Σj=σj2I\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}Σj​=σj2​I, kkk parameters), diagonal (kpkpkp), tied (one full matrix shared by the components, p(p+1)/2p(p+1)/2p(p+1)/2) or full (kp(p+1)/2kp(p+1)/2kp(p+1)/2), on top of the k−1k-1k−1 weights and the kpkpkp means. Comparing models with different numbers of parameters by the likelihood alone would always favor the largest, so we use the Bayesian information criterion BIC=−2ℓ(θ^)+dln⁡n\mathrm{BIC}=-2\ell(\hat\theta)+d\ln nBIC=−2ℓ(θ^)+dlnn, with ddd the number of parameters (smaller is better; this is the convention of scikit-learn and of the CpC_pCp​/BIC comparison of Section 10.3).

The following code implements EM, checks that the likelihood is monotone and that the result agrees with scikit-learn started from the same parameters, and shows what a mixture with full covariances does that kkk-means does not on Iris.

def em_gmm(X, pi, mu, Sigma, max_iter=500, tol=1e-10, reg=1e-6):
    """EM for a Gaussian mixture with full covariances: E-step (12.4), M-step (12.5)."""
    n, p = X.shape
    ll_hist = []
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        log_p = np.column_stack([np.log(pi[j]) + multivariate_normal(mu[j], Sigma[j], allow_singular=True).logpdf(X) for j in range(len(pi))])
        ll_i = logsumexp(log_p, axis=1)
        ll_hist.append(float(ll_i.sum()))
        R = np.exp(log_p - ll_i[:, None])                                   # responsibilities
        if len(ll_hist) > 1 and ll_hist[-1] - ll_hist[-2] < tol:
            break
        N = R.sum(axis=0)
        pi, mu = N / n, (R.T @ X) / N[:, None]
        Sigma = np.array([(R[:, j, None] * (X - mu[j])).T @ (X - mu[j]) / N[j] + reg * np.eye(p) for j in range(len(pi))])
    return pi, mu, Sigma, np.array(ll_hist), R


km3 = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X_iris)
pi0 = np.bincount(km3.labels_) / len(X_iris)
mu0 = km3.cluster_centers_
Sig0 = np.array([np.cov(X_iris[km3.labels_ == j].T, bias=True) + 1e-6 * np.eye(4) for j in range(3)])
pi_, mu_, Sig_, ll_hist, R_ = em_gmm(X_iris, pi0, mu0, Sig0)
sk = GaussianMixture(3, covariance_type="full", weights_init=pi0, means_init=mu0, precisions_init=np.linalg.inv(Sig0),
                     reg_covar=1e-6, tol=1e-10, max_iter=500).fit(X_iris)
print(f"EM from the k-means solution: {len(ll_hist)} E-steps, log-likelihood {ll_hist[0]:.3f} -> {ll_hist[-1]:.3f}, "
      f"never decreases: {bool(np.all(np.diff(ll_hist) > -1e-9))}")
print(f"scikit-learn from the same start: log-likelihood {sk.score(X_iris) * len(X_iris):.3f}; "
      f"largest difference of the means {np.abs(np.sort(sk.means_, axis=0) - np.sort(mu_, axis=0)).max():.1e}; "
      f"ARI between the two sets of hard assignments {adjusted_rand_score(R_.argmax(1), sk.predict(X_iris)):.3f}")
print(f"weights {np.round(pi_, 3)};  mean largest responsibility {R_.max(axis=1).mean():.3f};  examples with largest responsibility < 0.9: {int((R_.max(axis=1) < 0.9).sum())}")
print(f"ARI with the species: k-means {adjusted_rand_score(y_iris, km3.labels_):.3f}, mixture with full covariances {adjusted_rand_score(y_iris, R_.argmax(1)):.3f}")

Theorem 12.11 is confirmed: the log-likelihood rises from -197.320 at the kkk-means start to -180.185 and never decreases over the 41 E-steps (Figure 12.9(a) shows that most of the increase takes place in the first fifteen). Our implementation and scikit-learn, started from the same parameters, reach the same log-likelihood, with means that agree to 8×10−78\times10^{-7}8×10−7 (the tolerance of the stopping rule) and the same hard assignments.

The soft assignments are nearly hard: the mean of the largest responsibility is 0.990 and only 3 of the 150 flowers have a largest responsibility below 0.9, the flowers at the boundary between versicolor and virginica. What the mixture changes is the shape of the groups, and it matters for the result. The ARI with the species is 0.904 for the mixture with full covariances, against 0.730 for kkk-means. The estimated weights (0.299, 0.333, 0.367, that is about 45, 50 and 55 flowers) are close to the true proportions, while the sizes of the kkk-means clusters (62, 50, 38) are not: with equal spherical clusters the boundary between versicolor and virginica is the perpendicular bisector of the two centers, and it cuts through the more spread-out virginica group; with a covariance for each component the boundary can bend around it.

The likelihood of a mixture with free covariances has a flaw that the monotonicity theorem does not remove: it is unbounded. Center one component on a single example and shrink its covariance: the density of that example grows without limit while the other examples are explained by the other components. We check this on Iris, with a two-component mixture in which the first component is a Gaussian N(x1,εI)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_1,\varepsilon\mathbf{I})N(x1​,εI) centered on one flower and the second is fitted to the other 149.

p_dim = X_iris.shape[1]
rest = X_iris[1:]
comp2 = multivariate_normal(rest.mean(axis=0), np.cov(rest.T, bias=True))
log_comp2 = comp2.logpdf(X_iris)
rows = []
for eps in [1.0, 1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-8, 1e-16, 1e-32, 1e-48, 1e-64]:
    # log N(x; x_1, eps I), written out so that it can be evaluated for tiny eps
    log_comp1 = -0.5 * p_dim * np.log(2 * np.pi * eps) - ((X_iris - X_iris[0]) ** 2).sum(axis=1) / (2 * eps)
    ll = logsumexp([np.log(1 / 150) + log_comp1, np.log(149 / 150) + log_comp2], axis=0).sum()
    rows.append({"variance of the first component": f"{eps:.0e}", "log-likelihood": ll})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2f}"))
print(f"for comparison, the well-behaved 3-component mixture above has log-likelihood {ll_hist[-1]:.2f}")

The log-likelihood of this model grows without limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to0ε→0: from -380.77 with ε=1\varepsilon=1ε=1 to -93.25 with ε=10−64\varepsilon=10^{-64}ε=10−64, by 73.7 for every sixteen orders of magnitude of ε\varepsilonε (the density at the flower x1\mathbf{x}_1x1​ is (2πε)−p/2(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-p/2}(2πε)−p/2 with p=4p=4p=4, whose logarithm increases by p2ln⁡1016=73.7\frac p2\ln10^{16}=73.72p​ln1016=73.7), apart from a small dip at moderate ε\varepsilonε before the spike takes over. Between ε=10−32\varepsilon=10^{-32}ε=10−32 and 10-48 the model passes the log-likelihood of the sensible three-component mixture (-180.19) and then leaves it far behind. A mixture that describes one flower with a spike and the other 149 with a single Gaussian has a larger likelihood than the one that finds the species, so the supremum of ℓ\ellℓ is +∞+\infty+∞ and maximum likelihood has no solution to look for. What EM finds, when it does not collapse onto a spike, is a local maximum, and the likelihood of a fitted mixture is therefore not an absolute measure of quality.

Implementations avoid this by adding a small multiple of the identity to every covariance (the reg_covar of scikit-learn, the reg of our code) and by restarting when a component collapses; the likelihood is then a quantity to be compared among reasonable local maxima. We now let the BIC choose the covariance structure and the number of components, on Iris and on Wine (standardized).

bic_study = {}
for name, kmax in [("Iris", 6), ("Wine", 6)]:
    X, y = datasets[name]
    res = {}
    for cov in ["spherical", "diag", "tied", "full"]:
        fits = [GaussianMixture(k, covariance_type=cov, n_init=5, random_state=SEED).fit(X) for k in range(1, kmax + 1)]
        res[cov] = {"bic": np.array([g.bic(X) for g in fits]), "ari": np.array([adjusted_rand_score(y, g.predict(X)) for g in fits])}
    bic_study[name] = res
    table = pd.DataFrame({f"{cov} BIC": r["bic"] for cov, r in res.items()}, index=range(1, kmax + 1))
    table.index.name = "k"
    print(f"\n{name}: BIC (smaller is better)")
    print(table.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"))
    best = min(((r["bic"][k], cov, k + 1) for cov, r in res.items() for k in range(kmax)))
    print(f"best BIC: {best[0]:.1f} for covariance '{best[1]}' with k = {best[2]} (ARI with the labels {res[best[1]]['ari'][best[2] - 1]:.3f});"
          f"   ARI at k = 3: " + ", ".join(f"{cov} {r['ari'][2]:.3f}" for cov, r in res.items()))

Iris. The smallest BIC is 574.0 for a mixture of two components with full covariances (the partition is setosa against the rest: ARI with the species 0.568), as for the silhouette and the stability of Section 12.5. The model with three components and full covariances follows at 580.9, a difference of 6.9, which on the scale of Kass and Raftery (1995, differences of 6 to 10 count as strong evidence) is a clear but not overwhelming preference for two. The covariance structure matters more than the number of components: with spherical or diagonal covariances the BIC at k=3k=3k=3 is 853.8 and 744.6, much worse than for a full or tied matrix (580.9 and 633.8), because the four features are strongly correlated within each species. The ARI at k=3k=3k=3 confirms it: 0.730 (spherical, equal to kkk-means), 0.745 (diagonal), 0.886 (tied) and 0.904 (full).

Wine. The smallest BIC is 5476.5, for diagonal covariances and k=4k=4k=4 components, a model whose ARI with the cultivars is only 0.683: the fourth component divides one cultivar. With k=3k=3k=3 the BIC prefers the diagonal structure (5543.4, ARI 0.915) to the spherical (5708.8), the tied (5570.9) and the full one (5806.3). The full covariances are heavily penalized: a component has 13⋅14/2=9113\cdot14/2=9113⋅14/2=91 covariance parameters, and a cultivar has about 60 wines. The best ARI at k=3k=3k=3 is 0.946, obtained with tied covariances, which is not the model chosen by the BIC.

Two lessons follow. The BIC answers the question of density estimation (“which model describes the distribution of the features best, after a penalty?”), and it is not guaranteed to select the model that agrees with a grouping defined by other means. And its choice depends on the family of models searched: with full covariances only, Iris has two components and Wine has two.

def figure_12_8():
    Xp = X_iris[:, 2:4]
    km_p = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(Xp)
    gm_p = GaussianMixture(3, covariance_type="full", n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(Xp)
    markers = ["o", "s", "^"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    def match_to_species(lab):
        """Rename the clusters so that each takes the color of the species it overlaps most (colors only; nothing is recomputed)."""
        table = pd.crosstab(y_iris, lab).reindex(index=range(3), columns=range(3), fill_value=0).to_numpy()
        rows_, cols_ = linear_sum_assignment(-table)
        perm = np.empty(3, int)
        perm[cols_] = rows_
        return perm[lab]
    lab_km, lab_gm = match_to_species(km_p.labels_), match_to_species(gm_p.predict(Xp))
    parts = [("species (not used by the algorithms)", y_iris, None),
             (f"k-means, k = 3 (ARI {adjusted_rand_score(y_iris, km_p.labels_):.2f})", lab_km, None),
             (f"Gaussian mixture, full covariances (ARI {adjusted_rand_score(y_iris, gm_p.predict(Xp)):.2f})", lab_gm, gm_p)]
    for ax, (title, lab, gm) in zip(axes, parts):
        for s in range(3):
            m = y_iris == s
            ax.scatter(Xp[m, 0], Xp[m, 1], c=[CLUSTER_COLORS[a] for a in lab[m]] if lab is not y_iris else CLUSTER_COLORS[s],
                       marker=markers[s], s=28, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
        if gm is not None:
            for mu, S, c in zip(gm.means_, gm.covariances_, range(3)):
                w, V = np.linalg.eigh(S)
                ang = np.degrees(np.arctan2(V[1, 1], V[0, 1]))
                ax.add_patch(Ellipse(mu, 4 * np.sqrt(w[1]), 4 * np.sqrt(w[0]), angle=ang, fill=False, edgecolor="black", linewidth=1.4))
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlabel("petal length (cm)")
        ax.grid(False)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("petal width (cm)")
    fig.suptitle("Iris, the two petal features only (marker = species, color = cluster)", fontsize=11.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_8()

Figure 12.8 shows the difference on the two petal features, which are enough to draw it: in the central panel the partition of kkk-means (ARI 0.89 on these two features) has boundaries that are straight lines, and in the right panel the mixture with full covariances (ARI 0.92) describes versicolor by a narrow ellipse along the diagonal and virginica by a larger one, which is what the species look like. Figure 12.9 collects the likelihood and the BIC. In (a) the log-likelihood of EM rises quickly and flattens (Iris, k=3k=3k=3, full covariances). In (b) and (c) the BIC is plotted against kkk for the four covariance structures, with the vertical axis cut to show the region of the minimum (for Iris the spherical and diagonal curves are far above at small kkk): the curve of the full covariances is the lowest at k=2k=2k=2 in (b) and the highest at large kkk in (c), where the number of parameters grows fastest.

12.7.2 Hierarchical clustering and Ward’s criterion¶

A second way to avoid choosing kkk in advance is to build the whole family of partitions. Agglomerative clustering starts from the nnn examples as nnn clusters and repeatedly merges the two clusters that are closest, until one cluster is left; the record of the merges, with the distance at which each took place, is a dendrogram, and cutting it at a height gives a partition into any number of clusters, nested in the others. What “closest” means for two clusters AAA and BBB is the linkage:

linkagedistance between AAA and BBBtends to produce
singlemin⁡a∈A,b∈B∥a−b∥\min_{\mathbf{a}\in A,\mathbf{b}\in B}\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVertmina∈A,b∈B​∥a−b∥long, thin chains; isolates outliers
completemax⁡a∈A,b∈B∥a−b∥\max_{\mathbf{a}\in A,\mathbf{b}\in B}\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVertmaxa∈A,b∈B​∥a−b∥compact clusters of similar diameter
average1nAnB∑a∈A,b∈B∥a−b∥\frac1{n_An_B}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in A,\mathbf{b}\in B}\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVertnA​nB​1​∑a∈A,b∈B​∥a−b∥in between
Wardincrease of SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ caused by the mergecompact clusters of similar size

The last row is the one that connects with the rest of the chapter, and it is Proposition 12.2(b).

Proposition 12.13 (Ward’s criterion is the kkk-means objective)

The merge cost of Ward’s method is Δ(A,B)=SS(A∪B)−SS(A)−SS(B)=nAnBnA+nB∥μA−μB∥2\Delta(A,B)=\mathrm{SS}(A\cup B)-\mathrm{SS}(A)-\mathrm{SS}(B)=\frac{n_An_B}{n_A+n_B}\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2Δ(A,B)=SS(A∪B)−SS(A)−SS(B)=nA​+nB​nA​nB​​∥μA​−μB​∥2 by (12.2): at each step Ward’s method makes the merge that increases the within-cluster scatter the least, so it is a greedy, bottom-up minimization of the kkk-means objective, whereas Lloyd’s algorithm is an iterative improvement of a partition into a fixed number of clusters. The height of a merge in the dendrogram of SciPy is 2Δ(A,B)\sqrt{2\Delta(A,B)}2Δ(A,B)​.

Single linkage has a different structure, which explains its chaining.

Proposition 12.14 (single linkage and the minimum spanning tree)

The partition into kkk clusters obtained by single linkage is the partition into connected components of the minimum spanning tree of the complete graph of the examples (edge weights = distances) after the k−1k-1k−1 heaviest edges have been removed.

Proof. Kruskal’s algorithm builds the minimum spanning tree by examining the edges in increasing order of weight and adding an edge when it joins two different components; the components at each stage are exactly the clusters of single linkage, which merges the two clusters at the smallest distance between any of their members. Stopping when kkk components remain means leaving out the k−1k-1k−1 heaviest edges of the tree. ■\blacksquare■

A cluster of single linkage is therefore a set connected by a chain of short steps, whatever its shape: this is why the method finds elongated clusters that kkk-means cannot (Section 12.8), and why one outlier or a thin bridge of points between two groups is enough to merge them. The cost of the standard algorithms is O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) memory for the matrix of distances and between O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) and O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) time, which restricts the method to data sets of a few thousand points. The code checks Proposition 12.13 on the merges of Iris, compares the value of SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ obtained by cutting Ward’s dendrogram with that of kkk-means, checks Proposition 12.14 on Wine, and compares the four linkages on Iris and Wine.

Z = hier.linkage(X_iris, "ward")
members = {i: [i] for i in range(len(X_iris))}
errs = []
for t, (a, b, h, _) in enumerate(Z):
    members[len(X_iris) + t] = members[int(a)] + members[int(b)]
    if t in (0, 50, 100, 140, 147):
        A, B = X_iris[members[int(a)]], X_iris[members[int(b)]]
        delta = len(A) * len(B) / (len(A) + len(B)) * ((A.mean(axis=0) - B.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum()
        errs.append(abs(h - np.sqrt(2 * delta)))
print(f"Ward merge heights against sqrt(2 n_A n_B/(n_A+n_B) ||mu_A - mu_B||^2): largest difference over 5 merges {max(errs):.1e}")

print("heights of the last four merges of the Ward dendrogram of Iris (the last one first):", ", ".join(f"{h:.2f}" for h in Z[:-5:-1, 2]))

rows = []
for k in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]:
    lab_w = hier.fcluster(Z, k, "maxclust")
    rows.append({"k": k, "SS_W, Ward cut": ss_within(X_iris, lab_w), "SS_W, k-means": KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X_iris).inertia_})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).assign(**{"excess of Ward": lambda d: d["SS_W, Ward cut"] / d["SS_W, k-means"] - 1}).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

# Proposition 12.14 on Wine: cut the heaviest k - 1 edges of the minimum spanning tree
mst = csg.minimum_spanning_tree(squareform(pdist(X_wine))).toarray()
edges = np.argwhere(mst > 0)
order = np.argsort(-mst[mst > 0])
for k in (3, 5):
    cut = mst.copy()
    for e in order[:k - 1]:
        cut[tuple(edges[e])] = 0
    mst_labels = csg.connected_components(sp.csr_matrix(cut), directed=False)[1]
    single = AgglomerativeClustering(k, linkage="single").fit_predict(X_wine)
    print(f"Wine, k = {k}: ARI between the MST cut and single linkage {adjusted_rand_score(mst_labels, single):.3f}; cluster sizes {sorted(np.bincount(single).tolist(), reverse=True)}")

rows = []
for name, k in [("Iris", 3), ("Wine", 3)]:
    X, y = datasets[name]
    for link in ["ward", "complete", "average", "single"]:
        lab = AgglomerativeClustering(k, linkage=link).fit_predict(X)

    rows.append({"data": name, "linkage": "(k-means)", "ARI with the labels": adjusted_rand_score(y, KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X)),
                 "cluster sizes": sorted(np.bincount(KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X)).tolist(), reverse=True)})

Proposition 12.13 is confirmed: the heights of the merges of SciPy agree with 2Δ\sqrt{2\Delta}2Δ​ to 7×10−157\times10^{-15}7×10−15. The last four merges of the Iris dendrogram are at the heights 32.45, 12.30, 6.40 and 4.85: the large gap before the last merge, the one that joins setosa to the rest, is the dendrogram’s version of the preference of the silhouette for two clusters.

Cutting Ward’s dendrogram gives a partition that is never better than kkk-means for the objective, as one expects from a greedy method, and never much worse: SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ exceeds the kkk-means value by 0.6%0.6\%0.6% to 2.8%2.8\%2.8% for k=2,…,6k=2,\dots,6k=2,…,6. (The kkk-means values are themselves local minima, found with ten starts.) The Wine rows of the last table show what the other linkages do. Single linkage and average linkage produce clusters of sizes 174, 3 and 1: they find outliers and chain everything else into one cluster, with ARI -0.007 and -0.005. Complete linkage gives clusters of reasonable sizes but an ARI of 0.577, and Ward 0.790, below kkk-means (0.897). On Iris the ranking is different: average linkage is the best (0.759) and Ward (0.731) matches kkk-means (0.730), while single linkage isolates two flowers (98, 50, 2). No linkage is uniformly the best, and the one that works on a data set depends on its geometry.

The check of Proposition 12.14 on Wine is exact: cutting the k−1k-1k−1 heaviest edges of the minimum spanning tree gives the same partition as single linkage (ARI 1.000) for k=3k=3k=3 and 5, and the partitions are those of sizes 174,3,1174,3,1174,3,1 and 172,3,1,1,1172,3,1,1,1172,3,1,1,1: the heaviest edges of the tree lead to isolated wines, which is the chaining effect of the previous paragraph.

Figure 12.10 shows the top of the Ward dendrogram of Iris (the last 30 merges; the numbers under the leaves are the sizes of the subtrees that were contracted). The horizontal line cuts it into three clusters, with the setosa branch on the left; a cut at any height between 12.30 and 32.45 would give two. The advantage of the dendrogram over a single partition is that it displays all the scales at once and lets the reader decide where the structure stops being convincing.

12.8 Spectral clustering¶

12.8.1 When distances to centers are the wrong idea¶

The clusters of kkk-means are Voronoi cells, which are convex; those of a Gaussian mixture are ellipsoids. Many groups of real data are neither: a ring around a disk, two interleaved crescents, a long curved ridge. What these groups have in common is connectivity: each example is close to some other example of its own group, even if the group as a whole is far from being round. Spectral clustering turns that idea into an algorithm by first replacing the data with a similarity graph, and then clustering the vertices of the graph.

The graph has the nnn examples as vertices and a symmetric weight wij≥0w_{ij}\ge0wij​≥0 on each pair, large for similar examples. Three constructions are common: the ε\varepsilonε-graph (weight 1 if ∥xi−xj∥≤ε\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert\le\varepsilon∥xi​−xj​∥≤ε), the fully connected graph with Gaussian weights wij=exp⁡(−∥xi−xj∥2/2σ2)w_{ij}=\exp(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)wij​=exp(−∥xi​−xj​∥2/2σ2) (the Gaussian kernel of Chapter 9), and the mmm-nearest-neighbor graph, with weight 1 if xj\mathbf{x}_jxj​ is among the mmm nearest neighbors of xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​ or the reverse, which adapts to regions of different density and is the one we use. Let W=(wij)\mathbf{W}=(w_{ij})W=(wij​), let di=∑jwijd_i=\sum_jw_{ij}di​=∑j​wij​ be the degree of vertex iii and D=diag(d1,…,dn)\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)D=diag(d1​,…,dn​).

Definition 12.5 (graph Laplacians)

Assume di>0d_i>0di​>0 for all iii. The unnormalized Laplacian, the symmetric normalized Laplacian and the random-walk Laplacian are

L=D−W,Lsym=I−D−1/2WD−1/2,Lrw=I−D−1W.\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{D}-\mathbf{W},\qquad\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2},\qquad\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{rw}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{W}.L=D−W,Lsym​=I−D−1/2WD−1/2,Lrw​=I−D−1W.

Part (a) is a smoothness measure: f⊤Lf\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}f⊤Lf is small when f\mathbf{f}f takes similar values on similar examples. We will use it twice, to derive the algorithm and, in Section 12.9, to propagate labels. The code builds the mmm-nearest-neighbor graph of Iris and of Digits, checks (a) on a random vector, and counts the zero eigenvalues of Lsym\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ (the same multiplicity as for L\mathbf{L}L by (c)) against the number of connected components.

def knn_similarity(X, m):
    """Symmetric 0/1 adjacency of the m-nearest-neighbor graph (an edge if either example is among the other's m nearest)."""
    A = kneighbors_graph(X, m, mode="connectivity", include_self=False)
    return ((A + A.T) > 0).astype(float).toarray()


def laplacians(W):
    d = W.sum(axis=1)
    L = np.diag(d) - W
    L_sym = np.eye(len(W)) - W / np.sqrt(d)[:, None] / np.sqrt(d)[None, :]
    return L, L_sym, d


W_iris = knn_similarity(X_iris, 10)
L_iris, Ls_iris, d_iris = laplacians(W_iris)
f = np.random.default_rng(SEED).standard_normal(len(X_iris))
quad = 0.5 * (W_iris * (f[:, None] - f[None, :]) ** 2).sum()
print(f"Proposition 12.15(a) on the 10-NN graph of Iris: f'Lf = {f @ L_iris @ f:.6f}, (1/2) sum w_ij (f_i - f_j)^2 = {quad:.6f}")

rows = []
for name, X, m in [("Iris", X_iris, 5), ("Iris", X_iris, 10), ("Digits", X_dig, 5), ("Digits", X_dig, 10), ("Wine", X_wine, 5), ("Wine", X_wine, 10)]:
    W = knn_similarity(X, m)
    _, Ls, _ = laplacians(W)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Ls)
    n_comp, comp = csg.connected_components(sp.csr_matrix(W), directed=False)
    rows.append({"data": name, "m": m, "connected components": n_comp, "eigenvalues of L_sym below 1e-10": int((ev < 1e-10).sum()),
                 "component sizes": sorted(np.bincount(comp).tolist(), reverse=True), "largest eigenvalue": ev.max()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

Part (a) of Proposition 12.15 holds to the digits printed (f⊤Lf=1442.093502f^\top\mathbf{L}f=1442.093502f⊤Lf=1442.093502 in both forms). The number of eigenvalues of Lsym\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ equal to zero is the number of connected components in all six graphs, and the largest eigenvalues (1.34 to 1.61) are below the bound 2. The components deserve a look, because they are the first clusters that the graph provides without any computation. The 10-nearest-neighbor graph of Iris has two, of 100 and 50 flowers: no setosa flower has a flower of another species among its ten nearest neighbors, and no flower of the other species has a setosa flower among its own, so the graph separates setosa by construction. The Digits graph with m=5m=5m=5 has two components, one of 27 images whose nearest neighbors in the graph all lie inside the group, and the rest of 1770; with m=10m=10m=10 the graph is connected. A graph that is too sparse produces such small islands, which are components but not clusters of any interest; the choice of mmm is a parameter of the method, and Section 12.8.4 shows how much it matters. The graph of Wine is connected for both values of mmm.

12.8.2 Graph cuts and the relaxation¶

A good partition of the graph cuts few edges of large weight. For A⊂VA\subset VA⊂V with complement Aˉ\bar AAˉ let cut(A,Aˉ)=∑i∈A,j∈Aˉwij\mathrm{cut}(A,\bar A)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in\bar A}w_{ij}cut(A,Aˉ)=∑i∈A,j∈Aˉ​wij​. The smallest cut is a poor criterion, because the cheapest cut is usually one that separates a single vertex with a few neighbors from the rest. Two balanced versions penalize small sets, with vol(A)=∑i∈Adi\mathrm{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_ivol(A)=∑i∈A​di​:

RatioCut(A,Aˉ)=cut(A,Aˉ)(1∣A∣+1∣Aˉ∣),Ncut(A,Aˉ)=cut(A,Aˉ)(1vol(A)+1vol(Aˉ)).\mathrm{RatioCut}(A,\bar A)=\mathrm{cut}(A,\bar A)\Big(\frac1{\lvert A\rvert}+\frac1{\lvert\bar A\rvert}\Big),\qquad \mathrm{Ncut}(A,\bar A)=\mathrm{cut}(A,\bar A)\Big(\frac1{\mathrm{vol}(A)}+\frac1{\mathrm{vol}(\bar A)}\Big).RatioCut(A,Aˉ)=cut(A,Aˉ)(∣A∣1​+∣Aˉ∣1​),Ncut(A,Aˉ)=cut(A,Aˉ)(vol(A)1​+vol(Aˉ)1​).
(16)

Minimizing them over AAA is NP-hard (Wagner and Wagner, 1993). The Laplacian turns them into eigenvalue problems when the discrete constraint is relaxed.

Proposition 12.16 (RatioCut and Ncut as Rayleigh quotients)

(a) For A⊂VA\subset VA⊂V define fi=∣Aˉ∣/∣A∣f_i=\sqrt{\lvert\bar A\rvert/\lvert A\rvert}fi​=∣Aˉ∣/∣A∣​ if i∈Ai\in Ai∈A and fi=−∣A∣/∣Aˉ∣f_i=-\sqrt{\lvert A\rvert/\lvert\bar A\rvert}fi​=−∣A∣/∣Aˉ∣​ if i∈Aˉi\in\bar Ai∈Aˉ. Then f⊤1=0\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{1}=0f⊤1=0, ∥f∥2=n\lVert\mathbf{f}\rVert^2=n∥f∥2=n and f⊤Lf=n RatioCut(A,Aˉ)\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}=n\,\mathrm{RatioCut}(A,\bar A)f⊤Lf=nRatioCut(A,Aˉ). For k>2k>2k>2 groups the same argument with a matrix H∈Rn×k\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}H∈Rn×k whose columns are normalized indicators leads to min⁡tr(H⊤LH)\min\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{H})mintr(H⊤LH) over matrices with orthonormal columns, solved by the kkk eigenvectors of the kkk smallest eigenvalues (Ky Fan’s theorem), and the relaxed solution is a matrix of real numbers that has to be turned back into a partition. The standard way is to treat the nnn rows of the matrix as new, kkk-dimensional examples and to cluster them with kkk-means.

Algorithm 12.1 (spectral clustering; Shi and Malik, 2000; Ng, Jordan and Weiss, 2001)

  1. Build the similarity graph W\mathbf{W}W and its degrees D\mathbf{D}D.

  2. Compute the kkk eigenvectors u1,…,uk\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_ku1​,…,uk​ of Lsym\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ with the smallest eigenvalues. Shi–Malik (normalized cut): use vj=D−1/2uj\mathbf{v}_j=\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{u}_jvj​=D−1/2uj​, the eigenvectors of Lrw\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{rw}}Lrw​. Ng–Jordan–Weiss: use uj\mathbf{u}_juj​ and normalize each row of the matrix [u1⋯uk][\mathbf{u}_1\cdots\mathbf{u}_k][u1​⋯uk​] to unit length.

  3. Run kkk-means with kkk clusters on the nnn rows of the resulting matrix; the example iii belongs to the cluster of row iii.

Why does step 3 work? If the graph has exactly kkk connected components, the kkk eigenvectors with eigenvalue 0 span the indicators of the components (Proposition 12.15(b)), so that all the rows corresponding to one component are equal (up to the scaling by D1/2\mathbf{D}^{1/2}D1/2 of the NJW version) and kkk-means separates them without effort. When the clusters are joined by a few weak edges, the graph is a small perturbation of that case, and the perturbation theory of Davis and Kahan says that the span of the first kkk eigenvectors changes in proportion to the size of the perturbation divided by the gap between λk\lambda_kλk​ and λk+1\lambda_{k+1}λk+1​. The rows are then close to kkk points, and kkk-means finds the groups. The same reasoning gives the eigengap heuristic for choosing kkk: look for a kkk such that the eigenvalues λ1,…,λk\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_kλ1​,…,λk​ are small and λk+1\lambda_{k+1}λk+1​ is clearly larger. There is also a probabilistic reading of the normalized cut: Ncut(A,Aˉ)\mathrm{Ncut}(A,\bar A)Ncut(A,Aˉ) is the sum of the probabilities that a random walk on the graph, in its stationary regime, steps from AAA to Aˉ\bar AAˉ and from Aˉ\bar AAˉ to AAA (Meila and Shi, 2001), so that a good cluster is a set from which a random walk escapes rarely.

We implement both variants. For two clusters we also check Proposition 12.16(a) on the graph of the two overlapping Iris species (versicolor and virginica; setosa is a connected component by itself in the graph of the whole data set, as the table above shows), and look at the sign pattern of the Fiedler vector.

def spectral_embedding(W, k, variant):
    _, L_sym, d = laplacians(W)
    ev, U = np.linalg.eigh(L_sym)
    V = U[:, :k]
    if variant == "njw":                                          # Ng-Jordan-Weiss: rows of U normalized to unit length
        V = V / np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    else:                                                         # Shi-Malik: eigenvectors of L_rw, v = D^{-1/2} u
        V = V / np.sqrt(d)[:, None]
    return V, ev


def spectral_clustering(W, k, variant="rw", seed=SEED):
    V, ev = spectral_embedding(W, k, variant)
    return KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit_predict(V), ev


# Proposition 12.16(a) on the 10-NN graph of the 100 versicolor and virginica flowers (setosa is a separate component, see above)
sel = y_iris > 0
W_vv = knn_similarity(X_iris[sel], 10)
L_vv, _, _ = laplacians(W_vv)
is_vers = y_iris[sel] == 1
nA, nB = is_vers.sum(), (~is_vers).sum()
f_cut = np.where(is_vers, np.sqrt(nB / nA), -np.sqrt(nA / nB))
cut = W_vv[np.ix_(is_vers, ~is_vers)].sum()
ev_vv, U_vv = np.linalg.eigh(L_vv)
print(f"versicolor against virginica on their 10-NN graph ({csg.connected_components(sp.csr_matrix(W_vv), directed=False)[0]} component): "
      f"cut = {cut:.0f} edges; n * RatioCut = {len(f_cut) * cut * (1 / nA + 1 / nB):.6f}, f'Lf = {f_cut @ L_vv @ f_cut:.6f}, f'1 = {f_cut.sum():.1e}, |f|^2 = {f_cut @ f_cut:.1f}")
print(f"second eigenvalue of L: {ev_vv[1]:.5f}, so the relaxation bound lambda_2 = {ev_vv[1]:.5f} is below RatioCut = {cut * (1 / nA + 1 / nB):.5f}")
pred = (U_vv[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
acc = max((pred == is_vers).mean(), (pred != is_vers).mean())
part_f = pred.astype(bool)
rc_f = W_vv[np.ix_(part_f, ~part_f)].sum() * (1 / part_f.sum() + 1 / (~part_f).sum())
print(f"the sign of the Fiedler vector recovers the species of {acc:.1%} of these flowers (the species were not used); "
      f"its own RatioCut is {rc_f:.4f} ({part_f.sum()} and {(~part_f).sum()} flowers), against {cut * (1 / nA + 1 / nB):.4f} for the species")

# Our two variants against scikit-learn on the 10-NN graph of Digits
W_dig = knn_similarity(X_dig, 10)
lab_rw, ev_dig = spectral_clustering(W_dig, 10, "rw")
lab_njw, _ = spectral_clustering(W_dig, 10, "njw")
sk_lab = SpectralClustering(10, affinity="precomputed", random_state=SEED, assign_labels="kmeans").fit(W_dig).labels_
print(f"\nDigits, 10-NN graph, k = 10: ARI with the digits: Shi-Malik {adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, lab_rw):.3f}, "
      f"Ng-Jordan-Weiss {adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, lab_njw):.3f}, scikit-learn {adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, sk_lab):.3f};"
      f"  ARI between our Shi-Malik and scikit-learn {adjusted_rand_score(lab_rw, sk_lab):.3f}")

For the graph of the 100 versicolor and virginica flowers the identities of Proposition 12.16(a) hold exactly: the vector f\mathbf{f}f built from the species has f⊤1=0\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{1}=0f⊤1=0, ∥f∥2=100\lVert\mathbf{f}\rVert^2=100∥f∥2=100 and f⊤Lf=240=n RatioCut\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}=240=n\,\mathrm{RatioCut}f⊤Lf=240=nRatioCut, the species cut 60 edges and its RatioCut is 2.40. The bound is respected, λ2=0.282≤RatioCut\lambda_2=0.282\le\mathrm{RatioCut}λ2​=0.282≤RatioCut, but it is far from tight: the sign of the Fiedler vector gives a partition into 62 and 38 flowers that cuts only 27 edges and has a RatioCut of 1.146, less than half that of the species. The best partition of the graph is not the partition by species, which overlap in the measurements; the Fiedler partition agrees with the species for 86.0%86.0\%86.0% of the flowers. It is a relaxation, the eigenvector is not an indicator and the bound λ2\lambda_2λ2​ is 4 times smaller than the cut that the sign pattern attains.

On Digits, the Shi–Malik variant of our code and SpectralClustering of scikit-learn, which solves the same problem on the same graph, give the same partition (ARI between them 1.000, ARI with the digits 0.757 in both cases). The Ng–Jordan–Weiss variant gives a different one with an ARI of 0.819: the two variants differ only in the normalization of the rows before kkk-means, and that choice is worth 0.06 of ARI here.

12.8.3 Nonconvex clusters¶

We now test the claim of the section on data where kkk-means must fail. The data of the next experiment are constructed (they are the one place in the chapter where real data cannot be used, because we need clusters of a known nonconvex shape): make_moons produces two interleaved half circles, make_circles two concentric circles, 300 points each with a little Gaussian noise. We compare six methods, all given the true number of clusters, except the density-based method DBSCAN (Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu, 1996), which has no kkk: it calls an example a core point if at least min_samples examples lie within distance ε\varepsilonε of it, defines the clusters as the connected components of the core points together with the examples within ε\varepsilonε of a core point, and labels the remaining examples as noise. Like single linkage, DBSCAN follows chains of near points, but it ignores the isolated ones.

Xm, ym = make_moons(300, noise=0.06, random_state=SEED)
Xc, yc = make_circles(300, noise=0.05, factor=0.4, random_state=SEED)
shapes = {"two moons": (Xm, ym), "two circles": (Xc, yc)}
methods = {
    "k-means": lambda X: KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X),
    "Gaussian mixture": lambda X: GaussianMixture(2, covariance_type="full", n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X),
    "Ward": lambda X: AgglomerativeClustering(2).fit_predict(X),
    "single linkage": lambda X: AgglomerativeClustering(2, linkage="single").fit_predict(X),
    "DBSCAN (eps 0.2)": lambda X: DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit_predict(X),
    "spectral (10-NN, ours)": lambda X: spectral_clustering(knn_similarity(X, 10), 2, "rw")[0],
}
shape_labels = {sh: {m: fn(X) for m, fn in methods.items()} for sh, (X, y) in shapes.items()}
table = pd.DataFrame({sh: {m: adjusted_rand_score(shapes[sh][1], lab) for m, lab in labs.items()} for sh, labs in shape_labels.items()})
print("ARI with the true grouping (constructed data):")
print(table.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
print("DBSCAN labels as noise:", {sh: int((labs["DBSCAN (eps 0.2)"] == -1).sum()) for sh, labs in shape_labels.items()})
ARI with the true grouping (constructed data):
                        two moons  two circles
k-means                     0.247       -0.003
Gaussian mixture            0.488       -0.003
Ward                        0.597        0.001
single linkage              1.000        1.000
DBSCAN (eps 0.2)            1.000        1.000
spectral (10-NN, ours)      1.000        1.000
DBSCAN labels as noise: {'two moons': 0, 'two circles': 0}

On the constructed data the result is the one that was announced. kkk-means and the Gaussian mixture, whose clusters are convex, fail: on two circles both have an ARI of 0 (they cut the circles with a straight line through the center), and on two moons kkk-means reaches 0.247 and the mixture 0.488. Ward’s method, whose clusters are also compact, gives 0.597 on the moons and 0.001 on the circles. The three methods built on connectivity, single linkage, DBSCAN with ε=0.2\varepsilon=0.2ε=0.2 and spectral clustering with the 10-nearest-neighbor graph, recover both groupings exactly (ARI 1.000), and DBSCAN labels no point as noise. Two cautions are in order. The data are an easy case for the methods that follow chains: the noise (standard deviations 0.06 and 0.05) is small compared with the distance between the two groups, whereas on Wine single linkage was destroyed by a few outliers (Section 12.7.2). And the success of DBSCAN depends on ε\varepsilonε and min_samples, which we did not tune but did choose knowing the scale of the data; there is no criterion in the algorithm for choosing them.

def figure_12_11():
    names = ["k-means", "Gaussian mixture", "single linkage", "spectral (10-NN, ours)"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(14, 6.4))
    for r, (sh, (X, y)) in enumerate(shapes.items()):
        for c, m in enumerate(names):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            lab = shape_labels[sh][m]
            ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=[CLUSTER_COLORS[a] for a in lab], marker="o", s=18, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
            ax.set_title(f"{m}\nARI {table.loc[m, sh] + 0.0:.2f}".replace("-0.00", "0.00"), fontsize=10.5)
            ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
            if c == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(sh)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_11()

Figure 12.11 shows four of the six methods. In the first two columns the straight boundary of kkk-means and the curved one of the mixture cut the crescents and the circles across; in the last two columns the clusters follow the shapes.

12.8.4 Spectral clustering on Digits¶

On real data the situation is less clear-cut. Figure 12.12 shows, for the mmm-nearest-neighbor graph of Digits, the first 20 eigenvalues of Lsym\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ (the eigengap heuristic), the examples in the plane of the second and third eigenvectors of the random-walk Laplacian, and the dependence of the result on mmm and on the variant of the algorithm, with the other clustering methods of the chapter as baselines.

rows = []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for m in [5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50]:
    W = knn_similarity(X_dig, m)
    n_comp = csg.connected_components(sp.csr_matrix(W), directed=False)[0]
    row = {"m (neighbors)": m, "components": n_comp}
    for variant in ["rw", "njw"]:
        lab, _ = spectral_clustering(W, 10, variant)
        row[f"ARI {variant}"] = adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, lab)
    rows.append(row)
spec_m = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(spec_m.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
base = {"k-means": adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X_dig)),
        "Ward": adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, AgglomerativeClustering(10).fit_predict(X_dig)),
        "Gaussian mixture, diagonal": adjusted_rand_score(y_dig, GaussianMixture(10, covariance_type="diag", reg_covar=1e-2, n_init=3, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X_dig))}
print("baselines, ARI with the digits:", ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.3f}" for k, v in base.items()))
gaps = np.diff(ev_dig[:20])
print(f"eigenvalues of L_sym (10-NN graph): {np.round(ev_dig[:14], 4).tolist()}")
print(f"largest gaps among the first 20: after eigenvalue {int(np.argsort(-gaps)[0]) + 1} ({gaps.max():.4f}) and {int(np.argsort(-gaps)[1]) + 1} ({np.sort(gaps)[-2]:.4f}); gap after the 10th: {gaps[9]:.4f}")
print(f"[{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s]")

eigenvalues of L_sym (10-NN graph): [0.0, 0.0028, 0.006, 0.008, 0.0092, 0.0121, 0.0127, 0.0184, 0.0207, 0.0336, 0.0372, 0.0548, 0.0643, 0.0715]

Spectral clustering beats kkk-means (0.667) at every mmm tried, by 0.05 to 0.16 of ARI, but the comparison with the other baselines is less favorable. Ward’s method on the raw pixels reaches 0.794, and only the Ng–Jordan–Weiss variant with m=7m=7m=7 and m=10m=10m=10 exceeds it (0.825 and 0.819, by 0.03 at most). The Shi–Malik variant is below Ward for all mmm (0.719 to 0.769). The dependence on the graph is not small and not monotone: the NJW score varies between 0.739 and 0.825 over the values of mmm, a spread as large as the difference between spectral clustering and Ward’s method, so a comparison of methods made with one value of mmm would be arbitrary. The cost is also larger: every value of mmm needs the eigendecomposition of a 1797×17971797\times17971797×1797 matrix, whereas kkk-means on the pixels takes a fraction of a second.

The eigengap heuristic does not find the ten digits. The eigenvalues grow from 0 with the largest gaps after the ninth (0.0128) and the eleventh (0.0176) eigenvalue, and the gap after the tenth is only 0.0035: the graph suggests nine or eleven groups, in line with the criteria of Section 12.5. A clustering does not discover the number of classes of a labeled data set, because the labels are not the only structure of the data.

def figure_12_12():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.9))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, 21), ev_dig[:20], "o-", color=BLUE, markersize=5)
    ax.axvline(10.5, color=VERMILION, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
    ax.set(xlabel="index j", ylabel="eigenvalue of L_sym", title="(a) smallest eigenvalues, 10-NN graph")
    ax.set_xticks(range(1, 21, 2))
    ax = axes[1]
    V, _ = spectral_embedding(W_dig, 10, "rw")
    for d in range(10):
        m = y_dig == d
        ax.scatter(V[m, 1], V[m, 2], s=9, color=CLUSTER_COLORS[d % 10], marker=["o", "s", "^", "D", "v"][d // 2 % 5], alpha=0.7, label=str(d))
    ax.set(xlabel="eigenvector 2", ylabel="eigenvector 3", title="(b) Digits in the plane of eigenvectors 2 and 3")
    ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=7, markerscale=1.4, loc="best")
    ax = axes[2]
    ax.plot(spec_m["m (neighbors)"], spec_m["ARI rw"], "o-", color=BLUE, label="spectral, Shi–Malik")
    ax.plot(spec_m["m (neighbors)"], spec_m["ARI njw"], "s--", color=ORANGE, label="spectral, Ng–Jordan–Weiss")
    for (name, v), ls, col in zip(base.items(), [":", "-.", (0, (1, 3))], [GREEN, VERMILION, PURPLE]):
        ax.axhline(v, linestyle=ls, color=col, label=name)
    ax.set(xlabel="neighbors m in the graph", ylabel="ARI with the digits", title="(c) the result depends on the graph")
    ax.set_ylim(0.50, 0.84)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_12_12()

In (a) the eigenvalues increase gradually, without a clear step at the tenth. In (b), where each point is an image placed by two coordinates of its spectral embedding, the zeros (on the right), the sixes and the ones (at the top) are far from the rest, and most of the other digits are crowded in a small region at the lower left: the first nontrivial eigenvectors single out the groups that are most separated in the graph and the others emerge in the following eigenvectors. In (c) the lines are the baselines and the markers the two spectral variants; the dependence on mmm is visible, and so is the fact that the best spectral values are close to the line of Ward’s method.

Two practical limits of spectral clustering should be added. The first is cost: the dense eigendecomposition used here is O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3), and for large nnn one computes only the kkk smallest eigenvectors of the sparse Laplacian with Lanczos-type methods (which is what scikit-learn does for large graphs), at a cost that is roughly linear in the number of edges for each eigenvector. The second is that the method gives labels only to the vertices of the graph: there is no centroid and no decision function, so a new example has to be handled by an out-of-sample extension (the Nyström formula of Bengio and colleagues, 2004, or the nearest labeled neighbors in the graph), whereas kkk-means and the mixtures classify a new point with one comparison to the kkk centers. Spectral clustering is also related to kkk-means in a way that links this chapter to Chapters 9 and 13: the kkk-means objective (12.3) can be written with the Gram matrix of a kernel (Exercise 12.2), and the eigenvectors of a normalized kernel matrix are what spectral clustering and kernel PCA compute.

12.9 Clusters, labels and semi-supervised learning¶

12.9.1 Three settings, three assumptions¶

In the supervised problems of Chapters 4 to 11 every training example has a label; in clustering none has. Between them lies the situation that is most common in practice: semi-supervised learning, with lll labeled examples (xi,yi)(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​) and u≫lu\gg lu≫l unlabeled examples xl+1,…,xl+u\mathbf{x}_{l+1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{l+u}xl+1​,…,xl+u​, because labels cost an expert’s time and inputs cost nothing. What can the unlabeled examples tell us? They reveal where the inputs are, the density p(x)p(\mathbf{x})p(x), and the density says something about p(y∣x)p(y\mid\mathbf{x})p(y∣x) only if the two are linked by an assumption (Chapelle, Schölkopf and Zien, 2006):

  • the smoothness assumption: two examples that are close in a high-density region have the same label;

  • the cluster assumption: the examples of one cluster tend to share a label, equivalently the decision boundary should pass through low-density regions;

  • the manifold assumption: the data lie near a low-dimensional surface, and distances should be measured along it (that is what the nearest-neighbor graph of Section 12.8 does).

These are inductive biases in the sense of Chapter 3, and the No Free Lunch theorem (Theorem 3.8) applies: no semi-supervised method can be better than supervised learning for all problems. When the assumption fails, unlabeled data can hurt (Cozman, Cohen and Cirelo, 2003), and we shall see an example on real data.

Protocol. Digits keeps the split of Chapters 6 to 11 (1347 training and 450 test examples, stratified, random_state=SEED). From the training examples we choose mmm labeled examples per class at random, m∈{1,2,5,10,20,50}m\in\{1,2,5,10,20,50\}m∈{1,2,5,10,20,50} (so 10 to 500 labels); the other training examples are used with their labels hidden; the test accuracy is computed on the 450 test examples. Each choice is repeated 30 times with different random labeled sets (the same sets for all the methods), and we report the mean and the standard error of the mean. The hyperparameters of the semi-supervised methods are fixed in advance and not tuned, because with ten labeled examples there is nothing to tune them on.

12.9.2 Propagating labels on a graph¶

Proposition 12.15(a) says that f⊤Lf\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}f⊤Lf measures how much a function f\mathbf{f}f on the examples varies between similar examples. A natural semi-supervised rule is therefore to look for the smoothest function that agrees with the known labels.

Proposition 12.17 (the harmonic solution; Zhu, Ghahramani and Lafferty, 2003)

Let the vertices be ordered so that the first lll are labeled, with values fl\mathbf{f}_lfl​ (for two classes the labels 0 and 1), and write L\mathbf{L}L, W\mathbf{W}W in blocks. Assume every connected component of the graph contains a labeled vertex. Then the minimizer of f⊤Lf=12∑i,jwij(fi−fj)2\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2f⊤Lf=21​∑i,j​wij​(fi​−fj​)2 over the vectors with the prescribed values on the labeled vertices is unique and is

fu=Luu−1Wul fl=(Duu−Wuu)−1Wul fl.(12.6)\mathbf{f}_u=\mathbf{L}_{uu}^{-1}\mathbf{W}_{ul}\,\mathbf{f}_l=(\mathbf{D}_{uu}-\mathbf{W}_{uu})^{-1}\mathbf{W}_{ul}\,\mathbf{f}_l .\tag{12.6}fu​=Luu−1​Wul​fl​=(Duu​−Wuu​)−1Wul​fl​.(12.6)
(17)

It is harmonic: fi=1di∑jwijfjf_i=\frac1{d_i}\sum_jw_{ij}f_jfi​=di​1​∑j​wij​fj​ for every unlabeled vertex, so that the value at a vertex is the weighted average of the values of its neighbors.

Proof. With f=(fl,fu)\mathbf{f}=(\mathbf{f}_l,\mathbf{f}_u)f=(fl​,fu​), f⊤Lf=fl⊤Lllfl+2fu⊤Lulfl+fu⊤Luufu\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{f}_l^\top\mathbf{L}_{ll}\mathbf{f}_l+2\mathbf{f}_u^\top\mathbf{L}_{ul}\mathbf{f}_l+\mathbf{f}_u^\top\mathbf{L}_{uu}\mathbf{f}_uf⊤Lf=fl⊤​Lll​fl​+2fu⊤​Lul​fl​+fu⊤​Luu​fu​, a quadratic function of fu\mathbf{f}_ufu​ with gradient 2(Lulfl+Luufu)2(\mathbf{L}_{ul}\mathbf{f}_l+\mathbf{L}_{uu}\mathbf{f}_u)2(Lul​fl​+Luu​fu​). Since Lul=−Wul\mathbf{L}_{ul}=-\mathbf{W}_{ul}Lul​=−Wul​ the gradient vanishes at (12.6). The matrix Luu\mathbf{L}_{uu}Luu​ is positive definite: for g≠0\mathbf{g}\neq\mathbf{0}g=0, g⊤Luug=f⊤Lf\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{L}_{uu}\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}g⊤Luu​g=f⊤Lf with f=(0,g)\mathbf{f}=(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{g})f=(0,g), which is 0 only if f\mathbf{f}f is constant on every connected component, and then g=0\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{0}g=0 because every component contains a labeled vertex where f=0\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{0}f=0. The harmonic property is the iii-th row of Luufu=Wulfl\mathbf{L}_{uu}\mathbf{f}_u=\mathbf{W}_{ul}\mathbf{f}_lLuu​fu​=Wul​fl​. ■\blacksquare■

For KKK classes one solves (12.6) with the one-hot label matrix in place of fl\mathbf{f}_lfl​, one column per class, and predicts the class of largest score. The solution has a probabilistic meaning that is proved in Exercise 12.5: the score of class ccc at vertex iii is the probability that a random walk that starts at iii and moves to a neighbor with probability proportional to wijw_{ij}wij​ reaches a labeled vertex of class ccc before any other labeled vertex. A close relative is the label spreading of Zhou et al. (2004), which iterates F←α D−1/2WD−1/2F+(1−α)Y\mathbf{F}\leftarrow\alpha\,\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{F}+(1-\alpha)\mathbf{Y}F←αD−1/2WD−1/2F+(1−α)Y and does not clamp the labeled vertices (the given labels may be noisy); scikit-learn provides it as LabelSpreading. New examples (the test set) are classified by the average score of their mmm nearest training examples.

We implement (12.6), check it against scikit-learn’s LabelPropagation run with our graph, and then compare six methods on Digits: logistic regression on the labeled examples only, 1-NN on the labeled examples only, cluster-then-label (kkk-means with 10 or 50 clusters on all the training inputs, each cluster labeled by the majority of its labeled members, and by the label of the nearest labeled cluster if it has none; a test example takes the label of its nearest centroid), self-training (fit the logistic regression on the labeled examples, add the unlabeled examples that it classifies with confidence at least 0.9 with their predicted labels, and repeat), label spreading (m=10m=10m=10 neighbors, α=0.2\alpha=0.2α=0.2) and the harmonic solution (12.6) on the symmetric 10-nearest-neighbor graph.

Xg_tr, Xg_te, yg_tr, yg_te = train_test_split(X_dig, y_dig, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=y_dig)
print(f"Digits split: {len(Xg_tr)} training and {len(Xg_te)} test examples")


def harmonic_propagation(W, lab_idx, y_lab, n_classes):
    """Equation (12.6) with one column per class (a tiny ridge keeps components without labels from making the system singular)."""
    n = len(W)
    unl = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), lab_idx)
    d = W.sum(axis=1)
    Y_l = np.eye(n_classes)[y_lab]
    F = np.zeros((n, n_classes))
    F[lab_idx] = Y_l
    F[unl] = np.linalg.solve(np.diag(d[unl]) - W[np.ix_(unl, unl)] + 1e-9 * np.eye(len(unl)), W[np.ix_(unl, lab_idx)] @ Y_l)
    return F


def harmonic_predict(F, X_train, X_new, m=10):
    """New examples: sum of the class scores of the m nearest training examples."""
    idx = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=m).fit(X_train, np.zeros(len(X_train))).kneighbors(X_new, return_distance=False)
    return F[idx].sum(axis=1).argmax(axis=1)


W_tr = knn_similarity(Xg_tr, 10)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
lab_idx = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.where(yg_tr == c)[0], 5, replace=False) for c in range(10)])
unl_idx = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(Xg_tr)), lab_idx)
F = harmonic_propagation(W_tr, lab_idx, yg_tr[lab_idx], 10)
d_tr = W_tr.sum(axis=1)
print(f"harmonic property: largest |f_i - sum_j w_ij f_j / d_i| over the unlabeled examples = {np.abs(F[unl_idx] - (W_tr @ F)[unl_idx] / d_tr[unl_idx, None]).max():.1e}")
y_semi = -np.ones(len(Xg_tr), int)
y_semi[lab_idx] = yg_tr[lab_idx]
Xi = np.arange(len(Xg_tr))[:, None].astype(float)
lp = LabelPropagation(kernel=lambda a, b: W_tr[np.ix_(a.ravel().astype(int), b.ravel().astype(int))], max_iter=100000, tol=1e-10).fit(Xi, y_semi)
print(f"scikit-learn LabelPropagation on the same graph: largest difference of the scores {np.abs(lp.label_distributions_[unl_idx] - F[unl_idx]).max():.1e};"
      f" same predictions: {bool((lp.transduction_[unl_idx] == F[unl_idx].argmax(1)).all())}")
print(f"50 labels: accuracy on the {len(unl_idx)} unlabeled training examples {np.mean(F[unl_idx].argmax(1) == yg_tr[unl_idx]):.3f}, "
      f"on the test examples {np.mean(harmonic_predict(F, Xg_tr, Xg_te) == yg_te):.3f}")

The solution (12.6) behaves as Proposition 12.17 says: the residual of the harmonic property over the unlabeled training examples is 10-10 (the tiny ridge of 10-9 in the code only matters for graphs with a component that has no label), and scikit-learn’s LabelPropagation, fed with our graph through a callable kernel, gives scores that differ from ours by 3×10−93\times10^{-9}3×10−9 and the same predictions for every unlabeled example. With 50 labels (5 per class) the harmonic solution classifies 94.1%94.1\%94.1% of the 1297 unlabeled training examples correctly, and 91.1%91.1\%91.1% of the test examples, which are not vertices of the graph and are classified by the rule of the 10 nearest training examples; the difference between the two figures comes partly from that out-of-sample step and partly from the sample (this is a single labeled set, whose variability is measured below).

def cluster_then_label(km, idx, y_lab, X_new):
    k = km.n_clusters
    lab = -np.ones(k, int)
    for c in range(k):
        m = km.labels_[idx] == c
        if m.any():
            lab[c] = np.bincount(y_lab[m], minlength=10).argmax()
    known = np.where(lab >= 0)[0]
    for c in np.where(lab < 0)[0]:
        lab[c] = lab[known[((km.cluster_centers_[known] - km.cluster_centers_[c]) ** 2).sum(1).argmin()]]
    return lab[km.predict(X_new)]


def semi_supervised_experiment(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, per_class_list, reps=30, extra=False):
    K = len(np.unique(ytr))
    W = knn_similarity(Xtr, 10)
    km_cache = {(kc, r): KMeans(kc, n_init=3, random_state=r).fit(Xtr) for kc in (10, 50) for r in range(reps)} if extra else {}
    rows = []
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", RuntimeWarning)       # LabelSpreading divides 0 by 0 for examples that no label can reach (see below)
    for per in per_class_list:
        for r in range(reps):
            rng = np.random.default_rng([SEED, per, r])
            idx = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.where(ytr == c)[0], per, replace=False) for c in range(K)])
            ys = -np.ones(len(ytr), int)
            ys[idx] = ytr[idx]
            acc = {"logistic (labeled only)": LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr[idx], ytr[idx]).score(Xte, yte),
                   "1-NN (labeled only)": KNeighborsClassifier(1).fit(Xtr[idx], ytr[idx]).score(Xte, yte),
                   "label spreading": LabelSpreading(kernel="knn", n_neighbors=10, alpha=0.2, max_iter=1000).fit(Xtr, ys).score(Xte, yte),
                   "harmonic (12.6)": np.mean(harmonic_predict(harmonic_propagation(W, idx, ytr[idx], K), Xtr, Xte) == yte)}
            if extra:
                for kc in (10, 50):
                    acc[f"cluster-then-label, k = {kc}"] = np.mean(cluster_then_label(km_cache[(kc, r)], idx, ytr[idx], Xte) == yte)
                acc["self-training (logistic)"] = SelfTrainingClassifier(LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=2000), threshold=0.9).fit(Xtr, ys).score(Xte, yte)
            rows += [{"labels per class": per, "rep": r, "method": k, "accuracy": v} for k, v in acc.items()]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def summarize(df):
    g = df.groupby(["method", "labels per class"])["accuracy"]
    mean = g.mean().unstack()
    se = g.std(ddof=1).unstack() / np.sqrt(df["rep"].nunique())
    return mean, se


t0 = time.perf_counter()
semi_dig = semi_supervised_experiment(Xg_tr, yg_tr, Xg_te, yg_te, [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50], extra=True)
order = ["logistic (labeled only)", "1-NN (labeled only)", "cluster-then-label, k = 10", "cluster-then-label, k = 50", "self-training (logistic)", "label spreading", "harmonic (12.6)"]
mean_d, se_d = summarize(semi_dig)
print("Digits: test accuracy, mean (standard error) over 30 random labeled sets; columns = labeled examples per class")
print(pd.DataFrame({m: {f"{c} ({10 * c} labels)": f"{mean_d.loc[m, c]:.3f} ({se_d.loc[m, c]:.3f})" for c in mean_d.columns} for m in order}).T.to_string())
print(f"[{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s]")

The graph methods dominate when labels are scarce. With one label per class, ten labels in all, the harmonic solution reaches 0.821 and label spreading 0.806, against 0.650 for the logistic regression and 0.649 for 1-NN, which have only the ten labeled images to learn from: the unlabeled images contribute 16 to 17 points of accuracy. The gain decreases as the labels increase, as it must (with all the labels there is nothing left to learn from the unlabeled examples): label spreading beats logistic regression by 0.053 with 10 labels per class and by 0.028 with 50, and at 50 labels per class it is equal to 1-NN on the labeled examples alone (0.976 against 0.974, a difference of the order of two standard errors, which says only that the labeled examples are now numerous enough for the plain rule).

The other three methods show how the assumption enters. Cluster-then-label with k=10k=10k=10 plateaus at 0.76 from five labels per class on (the standard error of each mean is 0.005): its predictor is constant on ten clusters, and the clusters are not the digits (their ARI with the digits is 0.667, Section 12.5), so that no number of labels can make it better than the purity of the clusters; this is the bias of a model that is too coarse, as in Chapter 4. With k=50k=50k=50 clusters the bias drops and the method beats both supervised baselines up to five labels per class (0.894 against 0.852 and 0.858), but it never reaches the graph methods, and from 10 labels per class on it is below 1-NN (0.909 against 0.914, and 0.922 against 0.949 with 20). Self-training does not help: it is identical to the plain logistic regression at one and two labels per class and worse from five labels on, by 0.009, 0.031 and 0.010 at 5, 10 and 20 per class. It adds the unlabeled examples on which the model is already confident; they are almost always labeled correctly, but they are the examples that the model classifies correctly anyway, and they come mostly from the classes that it already separates well, so that the labeled set grows unbalanced (Exercise 12.10). Last caution: the standard errors measure the variation over the 30 labeled sets; the test set of 450 images is the same for all the methods and has its own sampling error (about 0.01 for an accuracy of 0.95), so differences of that size between two methods should not be over-interpreted.

12.9.3 When unlabeled data do not help¶

The same comparison on two other data sets shows the role of the assumption. We standardize with the mean and standard deviation of the training inputs (labeled and unlabeled, which is allowed because no label is used) and use the stratified 75%/25%75\%/25\%75%/25% split of the earlier chapters (random_state=SEED).

semi_other, splits = {}, {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for name, X_all, y_all, per_list in [("Wine", wine.data, y_wine, [1, 2, 5, 10, 20]), ("Breast Cancer", bc.data, y_bc, [1, 2, 5, 10, 20])]:
    Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X_all, y_all, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=y_all)
    sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xa)
    splits[name] = (sc.transform(Xa), ya, sc.transform(Xb), yb)
    semi_other[name] = semi_supervised_experiment(*splits[name][:2], *splits[name][2:], per_list)
    mean_o, se_o = summarize(semi_other[name])
    print(f"\n{name} ({len(Xa)}/{len(Xb)} examples): test accuracy, mean (standard error) over 30 random labeled sets")
    print(pd.DataFrame({m: {f"{c} per class": f"{mean_o.loc[m, c]:.3f} ({se_o.loc[m, c]:.3f})" for c in mean_o.columns} for m in mean_o.index}).T.to_string())

The result on Digits does not carry over automatically.

Wine. The unlabeled wines help when labels are few: with two labels per class the harmonic solution reaches 0.944 and label spreading 0.916, against 0.880 for the logistic regression and 0.870 for 1-NN; the advantage is gone at 20 per class, where all four methods are between 0.922 and 0.979 and the logistic regression is nominally the best (0.979 against 0.977). With one label per class the advantage is not established (0.841 against 0.792, but a standard error of 0.026 for label spreading).

Breast Cancer. Here the unlabeled data do not help, and for label spreading they hurt: at two labels per class its accuracy is 0.809 against 0.857 for the logistic regression (standard errors 0.019 and 0.011), and it remains below the logistic regression for every larger number of labels (0.917 against 0.932 with five per class, 0.949 against 0.963 with twenty). The harmonic solution equals the logistic regression from two to ten labels per class and is below it at twenty (0.950 against 0.963); with one label per class it is catastrophic, 0.653 against 0.797. The diagnostic lines explain this case. The two classes are not two clusters separated by a low-density region: 7.7%7.7\%7.7% of the edges of the 10-nearest-neighbor graph join a malignant and a benign tumor, and 38.0%38.0\%38.0% of the tumors have a neighbor of the other class, so the cluster assumption is weak, and a linear model, whose assumption fits these data (Chapter 6), makes better use of the few labels. With a single labeled tumor per class the harmonic scores are nearly tied across the graph, and the predicted share of malignant tumors depends on which two patients happened to be labeled: on average 49.6%49.6\%49.6% of the unlabeled examples are called malignant, with a standard deviation of 37.6 points across the 30 labeled sets, against a true proportion of 37.3%37.3\%37.3% (with two labels per class the standard deviation is 17.5 points). Label spreading has a different problem: with one label per class it gives no score at all (the scores are not numbers) to 13.9 of the 143 test examples on average, those whose nearest training examples had received no label mass: the iteration stops after a few steps (five in the first labeled set) before the labels of two tumors reach 153 of the 426 training examples, and scikit-learn then predicts the first class for the test examples that depend on them. These two failures belong to the method, not to the data: with more labels both disappear, but the graph methods then remain at best equal to the supervised baseline. Unlabeled data are not a free gift; they are a bet on an assumption.

Figure 12.13 draws the Digits table (a) and the gain of label spreading over the logistic regression for the three data sets (b). The gain is positive for all label counts on Digits (from about 0.16 with one label per class to 0.03 with fifty), positive and decreasing to zero on Wine, and zero or negative on Breast Cancer (an advantage of 0.008, within the error bar, with one label per class and then -0.048, -0.015, -0.007 and -0.014).

12.9.4 Clusters as features¶

A second way to use unlabeled examples is to learn a representation with them. We replace x\mathbf{x}x by its similarity to kkk centers fitted by kkk-means without labels: the triangle encoding of Coates, Lee and Ng (2011) is fj(x)=max⁡{0, dˉ(x)−dj(x)}f_j(\mathbf{x})=\max\{0,\ \bar d(\mathbf{x})-d_j(\mathbf{x})\}fj​(x)=max{0, dˉ(x)−dj​(x)}, with djd_jdj​ the distance to the jjj-th center and dˉ\bar ddˉ the mean of the kkk distances, so that a feature is nonzero only for the centers nearer than average. The features then feed a logistic regression. With all the training labels the number of centers kkk and the penalty CCC are chosen by 5-fold cross-validation on the training set (inside the pipeline, so that the centers are refitted in each fold), and the test set is used once. With a few labels, the centers are fitted on all the unlabeled training inputs and the regression on the labeled ones, with k=100k=100k=100 and C=1C=1C=1 fixed in advance.

class KMeansTriangle(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Triangle encoding of the distances to the centers of a k-means fitted without labels."""

    def __init__(self, k=100, random_state=0):
        self.k, self.random_state = k, random_state

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.km_ = KMeans(self.k, n_init=3, random_state=self.random_state).fit(X)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        D = self.km_.transform(X)
        return np.maximum(0, D.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) - D)


cv5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
raw_cv = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)),
                      {"logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}, cv=cv5).fit(Xg_tr, yg_tr)
feat_cv = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(KMeansTriangle(random_state=SEED), StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)),
                       {"kmeanstriangle__k": [10, 50, 100, 300], "logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1]}, cv=cv5).fit(Xg_tr, yg_tr)

res = {"raw pixels, 100 labels": [], "k-means features (k = 100) from the unlabeled examples, 100 labels": []}
for r in range(30):
    rng = np.random.default_rng([SEED, 10, r])

print("\n10 labels per class, 30 repetitions (test accuracy, mean and standard error):")
