With all 1347 training labels, a logistic regression on the kkk-means features reaches a cross-validated accuracy of 0.9792 and a test accuracy of 0.9800 (9 errors in 450), against 0.9673 and 0.9644 (16 errors) for the logistic regression on the pixels: seven fewer errors, a difference that a test set of 450 images cannot establish alone, but that the cross-validation, on 1347 images, supports. The best number of centers is 300, the largest value of the grid, so a larger value might do better; the point is that the best kkk is far above the number of classes: as a feature extractor, kkk-means is not asked to find the ten digits but to cover the space of images with enough centers that each image is near a few of them, which is the quantizer of Section 12.6 used as a representation.

With 100 labels (10 per class) and the centers fitted on the unlabeled training images, the logistic regression on the features reaches 0.921 (0.004) against 0.896 (0.003) on the pixels, a gain of 0.025 from clusters learned without labels. It is a smaller gain than that of label spreading at the same number of labels (0.949, Section 12.9.2), so that, in this experiment, the graph method makes the better use of the unlabeled images while the representation has the advantage of producing a fixed feature map that can be applied to new images, to be fed to any classifier.

12.10 The methods side by side¶

We close the chapter with the same table for all the methods and all four data sets, with the number of clusters equal to the number of classes: 3 for Iris and Wine, 2 for Breast Cancer, 10 for Digits. This is a favorable setting, because kkk is the one quantity that Section 12.5 showed to be hard to find, and the labels are used only to score. The Gaussian mixture uses the covariance structure with the smallest BIC at that kkk (a choice made without labels), and the spectral clustering uses the 10-nearest-neighbor graph and the Shi–Malik variant.

rows, chosen_cov = [], {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for name, (X, y) in datasets.items():
    k = len(np.unique(y))
    labs = {"k-means": KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(X),
            "Ward": AgglomerativeClustering(k).fit_predict(X)}
    gms = {cov: GaussianMixture(k, covariance_type=cov, n_init=3, random_state=SEED, reg_covar=1e-2 if name == "Digits" else 1e-6).fit(X) for cov in ["spherical", "diag", "tied", "full"]}
    best_cov = min(gms, key=lambda c: gms[c].bic(X))
    labs["Gaussian mixture (lowest BIC)"] = gms[best_cov].predict(X)
    chosen_cov[name] = best_cov
    labs["spectral (10-NN)"] = spectral_clustering(knn_similarity(X, 10), k, "rw")[0]
    for m, lab in labs.items():
        rows.append({"data": name, "k": k, "method": m, "ARI": adjusted_rand_score(y, lab), "NMI": normalized_mutual_info_score(y, lab),
                     "silhouette": silhouette_score(X, lab) if len(np.unique(lab)) > 1 else np.nan})
side = pd.DataFrame(rows)

print(side.pivot_table(index="method", columns="data", values="silhouette", sort=False)[list(datasets)].to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
print(f"[{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s]")

No method wins everywhere. In terms of ARI the mixture is the best on three data sets (Iris 0.904, Wine 0.915, Breast Cancer 0.774) and the worst on the fourth (Digits 0.590, with the covariance structure selected by the BIC, the tied one); Ward’s method is the best on Digits (0.794, with the best NMI, 0.868) and the worst on Wine (0.790) and on Breast Cancer (0.575); spectral clustering is never far from the best (0.745, 0.896, 0.767, 0.757) and never the best. kkk-means is never the best by ARI, but it is within 0.02 of the best on Wine and within 0.12 on Breast Cancer and is cheap. The explanations are the ones met in the chapter: the mixture adapts to elongated and unequally sized groups (Iris, Breast Cancer), the compact spherical groups of standardized Wine suit kkk-means, and in Digits the groups are not compact in the pixel space, where kkk-means and the mixture do worse than agglomeration and the graph (a plausible reading, not one that the experiment tests).

The silhouette ranks the methods differently from the ARI. It is practically the same for all methods on a given data set (Iris 0.50 to 0.55, Wine 0.28, Digits 0.17 to 0.18), highest for kkk-means on Breast Cancer and Wine (and on Digits, where spectral clustering ties with it), and lowest for the mixture on Iris, Breast Cancer and Digits, simply because kkk-means maximizes a compactness that the silhouette also rewards, and the mixture does not. On Digits kkk-means has the highest silhouette (0.182) and one of the lowest ARIs (0.667): an internal score measures the fit to a geometric ideal, and the agreement with the labels is another matter. Each number comes from a single run with a fixed seed, so differences of a few hundredths should not be interpreted; the differences between methods that are decisive here, such as 0.59 against 0.79 on Digits, are larger than that.

12.11 Summary¶

  • The problem (Section 12.2). Clustering minimizes the within-cluster scatter SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ over partitions, a set of size S(n,k)S(n,k)S(n,k) (6.2×10706.2\times10^{70}6.2×1070 for the 150 flowers and k=3k=3k=3). SSW\mathrm{SS}_WSSW​ has a centroid and a pairwise form (Proposition 12.1, identical to 10-14), SST=SSW+SSB\mathrm{SS}_T=\mathrm{SS}_W+\mathrm{SS}_BSST​=SSW​+SSB​, and merging two clusters raises the scatter by nAnBnA+nB∥μA−μB∥2\frac{n_An_B}{n_A+n_B}\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_A-\boldsymbol\mu_B\rVert^2nA​+nB​nA​nB​​∥μA​−μB​∥2 (equation (12.2), the gain of a split in a regression tree). The problem is NP-hard. On Iris the species explain 86.9%86.9\%86.9% of the scatter, and the best three clusters, with SSW=78.85\mathrm{SS}_W=78.85SSW​=78.85, explain more than the species (89.30).

  • kkk-means (Section 12.3). Lloyd’s algorithm alternates two exact optimizations, decreases JJJ at every step and stops in finitely many steps at a fixed point, which is a local minimum (Theorem 12.4), reproduced by scikit-learn to 10-15. Fixed points can be improved by single moves (Hartigan), by about one part in 105 on Digits, a small amount next to the spread between local minima: the best value found is 0.9%0.9\%0.9% to 6%6\%6% below the values reached by three single random starts. kkk-means++ more than halves the failures of uniform seeding on Iris (19 bad runs in 200 against 49) and is better on Digits (37%37\%37% of the runs at the best value against 21%21\%21%), but not on Wine; the number of starts matters as much as the seeding. The scale of the features is part of the model: on Wine the ARI is 0.371 for the raw features and 0.897 for the standardized ones.

  • Evaluation (Section 12.4). The silhouette compares cohesion and separation (0.681 for k=2k=2k=2 on Iris, 0.553 for k=3k=3k=3); the adjusted Rand index counts pairs, does not depend on the names of the clusters, and has expectation zero under random labels (to 10-4 for 3 to 200 groups on Digits), while the NMI of random labels grows to 0.15.

  • How many clusters (Section 12.5). J∗(k)J^\ast(k)J∗(k) decreases with kkk (Proposition 12.8) and so does the held-out distortion (from 4.214 to 1.380 for k=2k=2k=2 to 400). The four criteria agree on Wine (k=3k=3k=3, apart from the gap rule, which gives 4) and disagree elsewhere: Iris gets 2 from the silhouette and the stability, 3 from the species, nothing from the gap rule; on Digits the silhouette and the stability peak at 9, the best ARI is at 11 and nothing points at 10.

  • Quantization (Section 12.6). kkk-means designs a vector quantizer, whose distortion falls with slope −2/p-2/p−2/p in log⁡k\log klogk (Theorem 12.9). On the photograph a codebook of 16 colors gives 27.4 dB at 6:16:16:1 compression, and the mean squared error of the codebook is 12 to 16 times smaller than that of the uniform grid with 8 to 216 colors; the slope gives an effective dimension of 2.7 for pixels in 3 dimensions, and 6.3 for Digits (to be read with the caveats of Section 12.6.3).

  • Mixtures (Section 12.7.1). EM alternates responsibilities and weighted Gaussian fits and never decreases the likelihood (Theorem 12.11); kkk-means is its limit for equal spherical components of vanishing variance (Proposition 12.12). The likelihood is unbounded (the spike of a component on one flower takes it past the sensible fit at a variance between 10-32 and 10-48). On Iris the full-covariance mixture has ARI 0.904 against 0.730 for kkk-means; the BIC picks 2 components for Iris and 4 diagonal components for Wine (ARI 0.683), not the species.

  • Hierarchical clustering (Section 12.7.2). Ward’s merge cost is the increase of the kkk-means objective (Proposition 12.13, heights agreeing to 10-14) and its cuts are within 0.6%0.6\%0.6% to 2.8%2.8\%2.8% of the kkk-means value on Iris; single linkage is the minimum spanning tree with the heaviest edges removed (Proposition 12.14) and chains: on Wine it gives clusters of 174, 3 and 1 wines.

  • Spectral clustering (Section 12.8). The Laplacian satisfies f⊤Lf=12∑wij(fi−fj)2\mathbf{f}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{f}=\frac12\sum w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2f⊤Lf=21​∑wij​(fi​−fj​)2; the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 is the number of connected components (Proposition 12.15, confirmed on six graphs); RatioCut and Ncut relax to eigenvectors of L\mathbf{L}L and Lrw\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{rw}}Lrw​ (Proposition 12.16, with λ2≤RatioCut\lambda_2\le\mathrm{RatioCut}λ2​≤RatioCut). On two moons and two circles kkk-means and the mixture fail (ARI 0.247, 0.488 and 0) and single linkage, DBSCAN and spectral clustering recover both groupings exactly. On Digits spectral clustering reaches an ARI of 0.72 to 0.83 depending on the graph and the variant, against 0.667 for kkk-means and 0.794 for Ward; the eigengap suggests 9 or 11 clusters.

  • Semi-supervised learning (Section 12.9). The harmonic solution Luu−1Wulfl\mathbf{L}_{uu}^{-1}\mathbf{W}_{ul}\mathbf{f}_lLuu−1​Wul​fl​ (Proposition 12.17, equal to scikit-learn’s LabelPropagation to 10-9) lifts the accuracy on Digits from 0.650 to 0.821 with ten labels, a gain that shrinks to 0.03 with 500; it is useful on Wine with two labels per class and harmful on Breast Cancer (0.809 for label spreading against 0.857 for the logistic regression with two labels per class; 0.653 for the harmonic solution with one), because its assumption does not hold there. Self-training gains nothing or loses, although its pseudo-labels are almost all correct, and cluster-then-label with k=10k=10k=10 plateaus at 0.76. Clusters as features (k=300k=300k=300 centers, triangle encoding) improve the logistic regression on Digits from 0.964 to 0.980 with all labels and from 0.896 to 0.921 with 100.

  • The methods side by side (Section 12.10). With kkk equal to the number of classes the ARI is best for the mixture on Iris (0.904), Wine (0.915) and Breast Cancer (0.774) and for Ward on Digits (0.794); no method wins everywhere, and the internal silhouette does not follow the ARI.

Which tool for which situation
situationstart withreason
compact, roughly round groups of similar size; features on one scalekkk-means with kkk-means++ seeding and several starts, features standardizedcheap, simple; the result depends on the scale and the start (Sections 12.3.4 and 12.3.5)
elongated or unequal groups; a probability of belonging is neededGaussian mixture with BIC to choose the covariance structure and kkksoft assignments and a likelihood; the BIC answers a density question (Section 12.7.1)
a hierarchy, or nothing is known about kkkWard’s agglomeration and a dendrogramall the scales at once; avoid single and average linkage with outliers (Section 12.7.2)

compressing vectors or images; a data-driven codebookkkk-means as a vector quantizer, kkk from the rateoptimal quantizer for the empirical distribution (Section 12.6)

the number of clustersseveral criteria, the partitions themselves and the purpose; do not trust one numberthe criteria disagree (Section 12.5)
scoring against known groupsthe ARI, not the NMI with many groupsSection 12.4.2

Data sources¶

  • Iris: R. A. Fisher, “The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems”, Annals of Eugenics 7(2), 179–188 (1936). Bundled with scikit-learn; all 150 flowers, the four measurements in centimeters (Sections 12.2 to 12.8).

  • Wine: M. Forina et al., “PARVUS: An Extendible Package for Data Exploration, Classification and Correlation”, Institute of Pharmaceutical and Food Analysis and Technologies, Genoa (1991), UCI Machine Learning Repository. Bundled with scikit-learn; all 178 wines, standardized (Sections 12.3 to 12.10).

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn; malignant =1=1=1, standardized; for Section 12.9 the stratified 426/143426/143426/143 split of Chapters 6 to 11.

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). Bundled with scikit-learn; all 1797 images of ten classes, pixels divided by 16; for Section 12.9 the stratified 1347/4501347/4501347/450 split of Chapters 6, 9 and 11.

  • The photograph of Section 12.6.2: china.jpg, distributed with scikit-learn (sklearn.datasets.load_sample_image), a photograph of a pagoda by danielbuechele (Flickr), retrieved in 2011 by Robert Layton and released under a Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 license.

  • Constructed data (flagged in the text): the two interleaved half circles and the two concentric circles of Section 12.8.3 (make_moons and make_circles, 300 points each, Gaussian noise of standard deviations 0.06 and 0.05, a feature of the experiment and not a property of any real data set); the four points of Exercise 12.1, the contingency tables of Exercise 12.3, the two triangles of Exercise 12.4 and the path graph of Exercise 12.5; and the random partitions and random labels of Sections 12.2 and 12.4 and the uniform reference data of the gap statistic (Section 12.5), which are draws from a random number generator with the fixed seed of the chapter.

12.12 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 12.1 ★★ — A fixed point of Lloyd’s algorithm as bad as one likes. (Constructed points.) In the plane let the four points be (±a,±12)(\pm a,\pm\tfrac12)(±a,±21​) with a>12a>\tfrac12a>21​, and take k=2k=2k=2. (a) Compute JJJ for the partition into the left pair and the right pair, and for the partition into the upper pair and the lower pair. (b) Show that both partitions, with their means as centers, are fixed points of Lloyd’s algorithm. (c) What does this say about the ratio of the objective at a fixed point to the optimal objective? (d) Start from kkk-means++ seeding. If the first center is (−a,−12)(-a,-\tfrac12)(−a,−21​), compute the probability that the second center is the point (−a,12)(-a,\tfrac12)(−a,21​) (the choice that leads to the bad fixed point), and its limit when a→∞a\to\inftya→∞.

Hint. (a) The mean of a pair is the midpoint, and each point is at distance equal to half the length of the pair’s segment from it. (d) The probabilities are proportional to the squared distances D2D^2D2 to the first center, which are 1, 4a24a^24a2 and 4a2+14a^2+14a2+1. For the second center on the other side of the first, check that Lloyd’s algorithm ends in the left/right partition.

Exercise 12.2 ★★ — The kkk-means objective with a Gram matrix. Let X∈Rn×p\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}X∈Rn×p have rows xi⊤\mathbf{x}_i^\topxi⊤​, K=XX⊤\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\topK=XX⊤, and let Z∈{0,1}n×k\mathbf{Z}\in\{0,1\}^{n\times k}Z∈{0,1}n×k be the indicator matrix of a clustering (Zij=1Z_{ij}=1Zij​=1 if i∈Cji\in C_ji∈Cj​) and H=Z diag(n1−1/2,…,nk−1/2)\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{Z}\,\mathrm{diag}(n_1^{-1/2},\dots,n_k^{-1/2})H=Zdiag(n1−1/2​,…,nk−1/2​). (a) Show that H⊤H=Ik\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{I}_kH⊤H=Ik​ and that J=tr(K)−tr(H⊤KH)J=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{K})-\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})J=tr(K)−tr(H⊤KH). (b) Deduce that minimizing JJJ over the clusterings is maximizing tr(H⊤KH)\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})tr(H⊤KH) over matrices of this form, and that relaxing H\mathbf{H}H to any matrix with orthonormal columns gives a problem solved by the kkk leading eigenvectors of K\mathbf{K}K (Ky Fan’s theorem), with value ∑j≤kλj(K)\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j(\mathbf{K})∑j≤k​λj​(K). (c) Replace K\mathbf{K}K by the Gram matrix of a kernel (Chapter 9): what is the resulting algorithm called, and how does the relaxation compare with the one of Section 12.8.2?

Hint. (a) ∑i∈Cj∥xi−μj∥2=∑i∈Cj∥xi∥2−nj∥μj∥2\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2=\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert^2-n_j\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2∑i∈Cj​​∥xi​−μj​∥2=∑i∈Cj​​∥xi​∥2−nj​∥μj​∥2 and nj∥μj∥2=1nj1Cj⊤K1Cjn_j\lVert\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2=\frac1{n_j}\mathbf{1}_{C_j}^\top\mathbf{K}\mathbf{1}_{C_j}nj​∥μj​∥2=nj​1​1Cj​⊤​K1Cj​​.

Exercise 12.3 ★ — The adjusted Rand index by hand. Two partitions of eight examples have the contingency table (3113)\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}(31​13​). (a) Compute the number of pairs together in both partitions, the Rand index and the adjusted Rand index. (b) Explain why the Rand index looks high and the ARI low. (c) Find a contingency table with the same margins whose ARI is negative and compute it.

Hint. With ai=bj=4a_i=b_j=4ai​=bj​=4 the sums ∑i(ai2)\sum_i\binom{a_i}2∑i​(2ai​​) and ∑j(bj2)\sum_j\binom{b_j}2∑j​(2bj​​) are 12 each, and (82)=28\binom82=28(28​)=28. The Rand index counts the pairs on which the partitions agree, the ARI subtracts the agreement expected by chance (Proposition 12.7(c)).

Exercise 12.4 ★★ — Two triangles and a bridge. The graph has the six vertices 1,…,61,\dots,61,…,6, unit weights on the edges 12,13,2312,13,2312,13,23 and 45,46,5645,46,5645,46,56 (two triangles), and on the edge 34 (the bridge). (a) Write the degrees and the Laplacian L\mathbf{L}L. (b) For A={1,2,3}A=\{1,2,3\}A={1,2,3} compute cut(A,Aˉ)\mathrm{cut}(A,\bar A)cut(A,Aˉ), the RatioCut and the Ncut, and verify Proposition 12.16(a) for the vector f=(1,1,1,−1,−1,−1)\mathbf{f}=(1,1,1,-1,-1,-1)f=(1,1,1,−1,−1,−1) (here ∣A∣=∣Aˉ∣\lvert A\rvert=\lvert\bar A\rvert∣A∣=∣Aˉ∣, so fi=±1f_i=\pm1fi​=±1). (c) Use the symmetry of the graph (look for an eigenvector of the form (a,a,b,−b,−a,−a)(a,a,b,-b,-a,-a)(a,a,b,−b,−a,−a)) to compute λ2\lambda_2λ2​ exactly and check that λ2≤RatioCut\lambda_2\le\mathrm{RatioCut}λ2​≤RatioCut; what does the sign of the Fiedler vector give?

Hint. (c) The equations for the vertices 1 and 3 are a−b=λaa-b=\lambda aa−b=λa and 4b−2a=λb4b-2a=\lambda b4b−2a=λb; eliminate aaa and bbb to get a quadratic equation in λ\lambdaλ.

Exercise 12.5 ★★★ — Harmonic functions and random walks. Let f\mathbf{f}f be the harmonic solution (12.6) for one class (fl∈{0,1}l\mathbf{f}_l\in\{0,1\}^lfl​∈{0,1}l) on a connected graph with at least one labeled vertex of each value. (a) Show the maximum principle: 0≤fi≤10\le f_i\le10≤fi​≤1 for all iii, and for several classes the scores of an unlabeled vertex are in [0,1][0,1][0,1] and sum to 1. (b) Let Pij=wij/diP_{ij}=w_{ij}/d_iPij​=wij​/di​ and hih_ihi​ be the probability that the random walk with transition matrix PPP started at iii reaches a labeled vertex of value 1 before one of value 0. Show that hhh satisfies the same linear system as fu\mathbf{f}_ufu​ and conclude that f=h\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{h}f=h. (c) On the path graph with 5 vertices, with vertex 1 labeled 0 and vertex 5 labeled 1, compute f\mathbf{f}f. (d) What happens to (12.6) if a connected component has no labeled vertex?

Hint. (a) Look at the vertex where f\mathbf{f}f attains its maximum over the unlabeled vertices: harmonicity makes it an average of its neighbors. (b) Condition on the first step. (d) Luu\mathbf{L}_{uu}Luu​ is singular, since the indicator of that component is in its null space.

Python (computational) exercises¶

Exercise 12.6 ★★ — Choosing kkk on Breast Cancer. Use the standardized Breast Cancer data of this chapter. (a) For k=1,…,8k=1,\dots,8k=1,…,8 compute J∗(k)J^\ast(k)J∗(k) (with 10 starts), the silhouette score, the gap statistic and the stability, as in Section 12.5. Which kkk does each criterion choose, and what is the ARI with the diagnosis at k=2k=2k=2? (b) Repeat the clustering at k=2k=2k=2 on the raw (unstandardized) features and on the features scaled to [0,1][0,1][0,1]: how do the ARI and the cluster sizes change? (c) Which features contribute most to the difference between the two clusters of the standardized solution, as measured by the difference of the cluster means in standard-deviation units?

Hint. Reuse gap_statistic and stability from Section 12.5. For (c) the cluster means of the standardized data are already in standard-deviation units.

Exercise 12.7 ★★ — Mini-batch kkk-means from scratch. On the pixels of the photograph (Section 12.6.2) with k=16k=16k=16, implement the mini-batch algorithm of Sculley (2010): start from kkk centers chosen by kkk-means++ on a subsample; at each iteration draw a batch of bbb pixels, assign each to its nearest center, and for each assigned pixel increment the count vjv_jvj​ of its center and move the center by μj←μj+1vj(x−μj)\boldsymbol\mu_j\leftarrow\boldsymbol\mu_j+\frac1{v_j}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_j)μj​←μj​+vj​1​(x−μj​). For b=100b=100b=100 and b=1000b=1000b=1000 record the distortion on a fixed random subsample of 20,00020{,}00020,000 pixels after 10,50,100,50010,50,100,50010,50,100,500 iterations, and compare with the distortion reached by Lloyd’s algorithm on the same subsample and with scikit-learn’s MiniBatchKMeans. Count the distance evaluations of each method.

Hint. A Lloyd iteration evaluates nknknk distances, a mini-batch iteration bkbkbk. Report the number of distance evaluations needed to reach a distortion within 1%1\%1% of Lloyd’s; do not report running times, which depend on the machine.

Exercise 12.8 ★★ — From EM to kkk-means. On Iris fit a mixture of k=3k=3k=3 spherical components with a shared, fixed variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and equal fixed weights (only the means are learned), by EM started from the kkk-means centers, for σ2∈{4,1,0.25,0.0625,0.0156}\sigma^2\in\{4,1,0.25,0.0625,0.0156\}σ2∈{4,1,0.25,0.0625,0.0156}. For each value report the mean largest responsibility, the number of EM iterations until the means move by less than 10-8, the ARI between the hard assignments of the mixture and the kkk-means partition, and the largest distance between the learned means and the kkk-means centers. Compare with Proposition 12.12.

Hint. The M-step for the means is the weighted mean of equation (12.5) with the responsibilities of the spherical model, rij∝exp⁡(−∥xi−μj∥2/2σ2)r_{ij}\propto\exp(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)rij​∝exp(−∥xi​−μj​∥2/2σ2); use logsumexp to compute them.

Exercise 12.9 ★★ — The bandwidth of the Gaussian graph. On Digits compute spectral clustering (Shi–Malik) with the fully connected Gaussian graph wij=exp⁡(−∥xi−xj∥2/2σ2)w_{ij}=\exp(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)wij​=exp(−∥xi​−xj​∥2/2σ2), with σ=c δˉ\sigma=c\,\bar\deltaσ=cδˉ, where δˉ\bar\deltaδˉ is the median distance of a point to its 10-th nearest neighbor and c∈{0.5,1,2,4}c\in\{0.5,1,2,4\}c∈{0.5,1,2,4}. Report the ARI with the digits, the smallest eigenvalues of Lsym\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ and the largest value of λ11−λ10\lambda_{11}-\lambda_{10}λ11​−λ10​ (the gap), and compare with the 10-nearest-neighbor graph of Section 12.8.4. Which values of ccc give a graph that is almost disconnected, and which give a graph that is almost complete?

Hint. Use np.linalg.eigh on the dense matrix; at n=1797n=1797n=1797 it takes a few seconds. For a small ccc the entries of W\mathbf{W}W are tiny except for the nearest neighbors, and for a large ccc they are all close to 1.

Exercise 12.10 ★★★ — Why self-training gains so little. On the Digits split of Section 12.9 with 10 labeled examples per class, implement self-training from scratch: at each round fit a logistic regression (C=1C=1C=1) on the current labeled set, label the unlabeled training examples whose largest predicted probability is at least τ\tauτ, and add them. Run 10 rounds for τ∈{0.7,0.9,0.99}\tau\in\{0.7,0.9,0.99\}τ∈{0.7,0.9,0.99} and, for 20 random labeled sets, record after each round the number of added examples, the accuracy of the added pseudo-labels and the test accuracy. Is the lack of improvement caused by wrong pseudo-labels? Answer with the pseudo-label accuracy, with the classes to which the added examples belong (for τ=0.9\tau=0.9τ=0.9: how many examples of each class have been added after the ten rounds, and how does the test recall of each class change?), and with the calibration of the first model (Section 11.10): at τ=0.7\tau=0.7τ=0.7, how many pseudo-labels of the first round are wrong and how confident was the model about them, and how does its confidence compare with its accuracy?

Hint. Keep the true labels of the unlabeled examples aside only to measure the accuracy of the pseudo-labels; the algorithm never uses them. Compare the test accuracy after the last round with that of the logistic regression on the labeled examples alone, for the same random sets, with a paired difference and its standard error.

What comes next¶

Chapter 12 produced groups; Chapter 13 produces coordinates. Everything in this chapter measured the closeness of examples by distances in the original feature space, and two of its results already pointed at the next topic. The slope of the rate–distortion curve of Digits (Section 12.6.3) says that the 64 pixels behave as a data set of far fewer effective dimensions, the statement made in Section 4.7.3 with the help of a principal-component analysis that was used before it was taught. And the relaxation of the kkk-means objective in Exercise 12.2 is solved by the leading eigenvectors of the Gram matrix, exactly the computation behind the spectral embedding of Section 12.8. Chapter 13 starts from the singular value decomposition, which already explained least squares and ridge regression (Chapter 6), derives principal component analysis as the best low-dimensional linear approximation of the data and as the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix of Chapter 2, uses it to remove noise, to compress and to rotate the axes of the features for the axis-aligned trees of Chapter 11, and extends it to kernel PCA with the Gram matrices of Chapter 9. After that the book leaves classical methods behind: Part IV (Chapters 14 to 21) builds neural networks, where a layer learns features instead of being given them, the autoencoder of Chapter 20 learns a nonlinear version of the compression of this chapter and of the next, and the graph Laplacian of Section 12.8 returns in Chapter 21 as the operator that a graph neural network applies.
